written.beta: Scramble to a cave below a roof crack that arches rightward, then jam and lieback it.
Once above the chimney, take the ramp up and rightward past the pin.
Four bolts protect it.
Step off the round boulder, clip the lone bolt, and complete the climb in the leftward-leaning groove.
Sustained crack climbing that stays clean and steep.
Begin in the little crack that bends rightward (the first bolt is right below it) and follow six bolts upward along the north side. Past the final bolt, bear leftward onto the shoulder.
A cut-off tree trunk partway up the crack makes the route easy to identify. The crack is wide enough in places to swallow a climber.

Expect thin fingers on pitch two, where the hardest moves surmount a bulge. Higher up you stem a shallow dihedral and swing out through a roof, then merge with the neighbouring route for the finish.

Pitch one starts mid-ledge, jams up to a slender corner, and gets over a roof with a single 5.9 pull.
Unbroken crack climbing on the lean-over northern corner of this tower. Link past the first possible hanging stance. The way down is a rappel east followed by the east ledges.

The traverse: from South Arapaho's summit, follow the connecting ridge north, about three quarters of a mile one way. Almost all of it is Class 3, with roughly 300 ft of downclimbing and 400 ft of climbing each way, including a somewhat exposed Class 3 downclimb of about 50 ft early on. Stay near the crest and escape to the west side at difficulties; the east side drops to the glacier. Occasional painted marks and cairns show the line but are sparse. The crux: about three quarters of the way to North Arapaho, two short steps of roughly 8-10 ft each go at Class 4 on good holds; some parties find a line that stays Class 3. Final slopes: easier ground, sometimes with a lingering snow patch, leads to North Arapaho's broad summit. Allow at least an hour each way on the ridge.
written.approach: From the Fourth of July Trailhead, take the Arapaho Pass trail past the Diamond Lake junction (about 1.1 mi) to the Fourth of July Mine ruins (about 2 mi). Turn sharply back to the northeast onto the signed Arapaho Glacier trail and follow it above treeline to the saddle on South Arapaho's southeast shoulder (about 12,700 ft), then scramble to South Arapaho's summit (about 4 mi from the trailhead). The scramble from the saddle to South Arapaho's summit is rocky and loose Class 2, passing a false summit.

written.beta: The start ledge is reached by a delicate downclimb. Face climb to gain the thin cracks, stemming the corner, then jam the strenuous finger-width crack as it trends rightward, finishing on gravelly easier rock.
A steep slab with a trio of fixed bolts plus a dike to use, ending at chained anchors.
A striking prow, found past a dead tree: a slim corner gives access to an arete with three bolts.
The opening moves are the crux and are difficult to protect.
Steep face climbing alongside a crack toward a belay point. Be aware that the one existing piton is poor.

Share the beginning with the neighbouring route Top Dawg, then veer leftward once you clip the first bolt, climbing a steep face of sidepulls and layback moves. Finish on the slab above, clipping the other route's anchors.
Chimney up the black slot a little right of another line. Use the anchors belonging to the neighbouring Cracking Up.
Start near Winds of Fortune and pull the roof using a square jug, then run up the face, bear left past a bulge, then end with a fist-width crack.
Protection is mostly fixed.

Start atop a boulder beneath the face. Move up and leftward to a small overhang, undercling rightward under it and lean back to a rest beneath a shallow corner. The corner holds the crux, then edge across leftward to a finger-width seam.

Crawl through the boulder tunnel to the dihedral and jam its crack, then make a tough exit at the crescent roof, leftward, to a bolted stance. Pitch two frictions up a bolted slab. A direct start edges rightward from the boulders past a line of bolts.
Tucked immediately behind a cluster of large firs, the route is a slim finger-width fissure.

Begin low on the ramp, beneath the big offwidth. Jam up the left side of the small pillar called the Rat's Tooth and squeeze to a piton, then step out leftward onto a flake for the belay. The next pitch wrestles through a slot of ten inches, then undercuts leftward to a stance.

Further body-jamming, easier at 5.10a, reaches a gentle ramp, and the top is easy in either direction.
Climb the steep slab to the right of a neighbouring route, face-climbing through thin, fractured crack systems and clipping three bolts.
Follow the huge dihedral that leans and arches leftward on the southern wall's right-hand edge.

Pitch one follows a pale, steep dihedral under a prominent corner, laybacking and jamming a thin crack of finger and hand size, with 5.9+ moves close to the top, to a big ledge with anchors.

Rappel there, or do the shorter second pitch, which swings left beneath the steep headwall before returning right above it.
Follow the good crack in the stepped corner that faces left over roughly 90 feet, then make a tricky traverse rightward to join a neighbouring route.
The first pitch climbs vertical rock rightward out of the gully with little gear, reaching a small stance. The second pitch follows an easy crack to the slabs near the summit.

The first pitch is the easy opening lead of the neighbouring dihedral route, up to a belay. The second jams cracks that widen from fingers to hands, just left of a dark streak, ending at a stance under a small tree.

On the last pitch, angle rightward and upward below a little roof, pull around it on its left, and continue over easier broken ground.

Start to the right of a neighbouring route. Climb an easy flake, then trend leftward into the inner corner of an enormous cleft, and fight up the overhanging crack above with strenuous fist jams to a ledge higher and to the right.

The second pitch trends rightward into an easier corner.
Fingertip laybacks up a short, steep bulge beside the big overhang make the whole problem. Above it, slabs continue: finish through the roof or cross rightward into the neighbouring crack system.

Begin on a thin crack slanting rightward, where the opening moves of dicey face climbing are the hardest. Stop on a little perch under the finger crack; splitting the route in two keeps rope drag down. Jam the crack to a flake belay, then rappel.
The line is the shallow dihedral in the northwest face, started from a broken pile of blocks.

Begin from the ledge halfway up the face, at its left side. Climb a handful of bolts, heading left initially and then right as you near the overhang. Pull over the lip, clip one last bolt, then finish up to the anchors.
Climb two rope-lengths of steep, overhanging rock up the west face.
written.approach: Come at the spire from its north side.

written.beta: Jam cracks up the corner that faces left to the tree standing on a roomy shelf. An optional second pitch climbs easy rock leftward beneath the arch before retracing the same moves back to the ledge.
A big flake rests against the face. Ascend the middle of it, or along its right edge, to a ledge with a tree.

Begin beside an enormous flake and follow the line of bolts to the steep headwall, where the moves reach 5.12. The two-bolt hanging stance sits within the crux section, so it works as a rest.

From the stance, trend up and left onto a crack that ends the route.
Work a grubby crack that angles rightward up into the east-side corner, then fight through the roof with hard jamming.
Go to the first bolt of the neighbouring Birdland, then face-climb beside a blunt edge on its left.

Start up some chopped footholds below a pointed buttress. The first pitch swings rightward around the buttress clipping old pitons, then enters a thin vertical crack where you jam the scars left by removed pins to a hanging stance.

Lowering off there is an option; otherwise head up and right via bolted-in pegs up to the top of the pillar.

Either use a groove beside a neighbouring route or layback up the boulder's left flank and cut left. Climb a flake to its crest, then trace a pale dike to a blocky stance; the bottom is run out over easy face climbing with little protection.

The upper pitch is a lovely thin crack to the ledge where you walk off.

Begin on a block or flake on the slab's south side and wander up and to the left, clipping a handful of old quarter-inch bolts, up to a belay beneath the arch.

Carry mid-size cams and large nuts to build the belay.

The line opens on the edge of a shallow flake that faces left, then trends up and leftward to a belay on the neighbouring buttress.

Next, tackle the leftmost of a pair of long finger cracks up to a perch on top of a flake, then a leaning dihedral reaches a large terrace. Scramble onward to the cave region and choose any finish.
Work cracks inside a corner that faces right using finger and hand jams plus stemming, arriving at the first belay ledge of the neighbouring Honey Pot route.

Pitch one is an easy ramp scramble, up and to the left, to a stance beneath the corner. Pitch two climbs the corner briefly, crosses toward an arete on the right, and resumes up the corner to another stance.

One long pitch beginning midway up the slanting flake beneath Borghoff's Blunder. Trend rightward to a dynamic move that forms the crux, then keep going past pockets and further hard bits. Fixed pitons protect the line.
Pitch one is free climbing to a ledge belay. Pitch two mixes free and aid up the crescent arch to a hanging sling belay, and the third hooks out and follows seams.
Follow the big obvious dihedral in two or three pitches. The hard part is a layback directly under the top belay ledge.
Usually toproped. Step into the shallow corner facing right on the dihedral's northern side.

Ascend the open book that leans left, going past the large roof near the face's right edge, which is the crux; a crack holding two pins then ends at a belay perched on a sloping stance.

Higher, shift left, jam a crack about two inches wide and exit rightward.

The first lead is a simple hand-width crack to a tiny stance under an upper corner. The second edges up that narrow corner on a thin crack, steps left onto an unprotected slab, and goes over the arch.
A hard, overhanging crack on the east flank of the wall. It also goes as an easy aid line.
Climb the large corner system leaning right in the wall's bottom right.
Work up the shallow corner leaning right beside Thug Route to the tree.
Start beside the big roof, go around its left side, then trend up and right over the stained seep line and some ledges to the three-bolt headwall.
A long crack system along the wall's right edge that takes five or six pitches. Head toward the large tree against the sky; the upper pitches trend left to reach it.

A zigzagging crack-and-corner line that bends over five roofs. Begin from a flake on the right and step left where the largest roof hangs.

The next pitch ascends the dihedral and crosses a roof on a fist-sized crack.
Follow a hand crack that leans, out at the westernmost end of the formation.
A lengthy bolted face climb with sustained difficulty up the steep right-hand side of the gully, in three pitches. Begin high in the chimney below a curving crack.
The big dihedral resembles a numeral 7. Climb up it and then get around the roof by going left.
A layback section and thin crack in the line east of the arete. It is easily toproped from the anchors of Brain Cloud.

The first pitch jams the right-hand crack at hand size to a comfortable terrace; the second takes a gentle, grassy crack up to a perch under the big roof, off to its right.

The third climbs a steep crack taking hands and fists on the roof's right side to a ledge shared with its companion route; the last two pitches angle up and right through broken cracks, corners and slabs.

Face climb to the roof, then hand-traverse and undercling leftward under smaller roofs to reach a steep slab. A bolt protects the harder variation straight above; the alternative swings right for the easier way.

Both versions end at a stance by a horizontal crack. Small and medium cams plus long slings help on the traverse.

The lower pitches work cracks and chimneys in a slim buttress, while the upper pitches tackle the steep headwall that caps the arete.

The line meanders, so choose whatever looks best as you go.

Start left of a wide crack and jam a thin, tight finger crack up to a ledge inside the wide crack. Next, head up and right through a shallow leaning corner, then traverse onto knobs and into a recess in the wide crack system.

Belay on a shelf up that crack. The final pitch is easier-angle but offers no protection.
A friction climb up the striking slab that slants right and cuts the face. Easy ground leads to a belay platform, then bolts guide you up in one or two pitches.
Follow two cracks side by side immediately left of the arete.

The first pitch jams a string of cracks to a belay on a diagonal crack. Next, angle leftward into an extended crack with some offwidth, then belay high at a sloping ledge.

The final pitch moves right and finishes by a mellow crack.
Take the seam leaving the left end of the ledge, then finish via a notch to the rappel station.

The first pitch goes up a fine hand crack, the center one of three obvious cracks, ending on a terrace; the crack on its left makes an alternate start. Next, a crack at a gentler angle slants left to a stance beneath a jutting roof.

Simple cracks past a block lead to good ledges, and the last two pitches keep slanting left through gentle cracks and corners to the summit.
Two thin cracks run side by side up the wall; begin them from the crest of the leaning flake.
Follow the narrow crack in the open book up to the slot.
Jam a finger crack and then a hand crack angling up and right, grunt through the offwidth, then chimney up onto a terrace.
A crack in the 5.8 range leads to a roof, with the headwall higher up protected by three bolts.
Start as for the neighboring Renaissance line, clipping a pair of bolts to reach a crack that bends leftward.
Start beneath the left end of the prominent roof at the corner, work up the shallow cracks, and carry on to the summit by sharing the finish of the neighboring South Side Classic.
Start to the left of a toppled tree and follow the obvious finger crack.
An overhanging crack that opens from finger size to hands.

The first pitch overcomes an overhanging offwidth for forty feet to a perch beside a big tree; you can also reach that perch by scrambling from the left. The second pitch follows a thin crack, then bears left and up across unprotected face climbing for seventy feet to a comfortable belay shelf.

The last pitch is a short crack and face section shared with a neighboring route.

Begin beside the large trees at the foot of the face. The first pitch works a broad crack up to a stance, continues in the crack and exits a flare into hand-size jams to belay.

The second pitch jams the corner that faces right, traverses under a clear roof and finishes with a superb hand crack to a roomy belay. The third is an awkward offwidth.

Scramble up talus beneath the west-side buttress to the foot of the two obvious cracks. The short first pitch works the pair of hand-size cracks, then makes a delicate traverse onto a ledge.

The second pitch climbs a short, broken corner overhead.

Jam the cracks for sixty or seventy feet but resist the leftward escape. You can fight over to a dangling flake, laybacking onto the fractured shelf, or keep going via the flaring slot overhead, the crux, to a large terrace shared with the neighboring East Ridge climb.
Start to the right of a tree and work the twin finger cracks to the shelf.
Angle up and right over slabby stone to a ledge, then cross a band of coarse pegmatite and wander up to the anchors. Thirteen bolts protect the line.

rack_items.sizes: double, if linking into one pitch

written.beta: A sustained line up the steep wall to the right of its neighbor. Step up onto a shelf to begin, clip the bolt overhead, and follow thin slanting cracks to a bolt on the upper slab, topping out on the cliff.
Pitch one is the sustained finger crack over several roofs. Pitch two continues in broader cracks from the ledge's right end, with a roof move near the start.

Start roughly thirty feet left of the neighboring Fat-Bottomed Groove, underneath a gap in the roof. Clip a bolt, reach that gap, then power across horizontal holds, using a bolt plus a pin, to a sandy-floored trough, the crux.

Keep going in the trough or shift leftward onto a fine crack ending at a belay ledge, then ease to gentler ground and exit eastward.

A strenuous, historic line on the tooth's northern aspect. Battle a broad jam crack (the crux), squirm into the chimney about forty feet up, then grunt to the belay atop Tiger's Tooth, where you choose a finish. Protection comes from nuts and fixed pitons.

The opening pitch jams a sustained finger crack for forty feet to a sloping dihedral. From there, either climb the corner and pull the roof above, or take the bolted arete on the left to a two-bolt belay and rappel station.
Link the cracks: begin up the corner, drift right where it bulges, then carry on up the dihedral above, finishing on easier ground.
Begin up the flake that faces left, trend up and leftward by an aging bolt, then follow narrow cracks plus two more bolts (the crux) up to the anchor.
Follow the corner crack; the climbing is smooth until difficulty arrives near the top.

Climb steeply up the ridge to around 10,200 ft, where it bends northwest, and continue up to about 10,800 ft. From here the ridge narrows and the scrambling becomes sustained: a series of short rock steps, roughly 10-30 ft high, around 11,000 ft form the crux, followed by long stretches of easier Class 2-3 scrambling to the summit. Stay on or very close to the crest, dropping just left of it when needed; the faces on either side quickly turn into Class 4-5 terrain.
written.approach: From Idaho Highway 28 in the Birch Creek Valley on the east side of the Lemhi Range, turn west on the signed Pass Creek Road (north of the old Blue Dome site). Beyond the first couple of miles the road fords Pass Creek and becomes rough; stay on the main track through a gate and into the national forest. The road finishes as rough jeep tracks to a small saddle with a fire ring at about 8,000 ft, where parties park. From the parking area, follow the remains of an old jeep track and then a worn climbers' path up grassy slopes to a saddle on the ridge at about 9,300 to 9,400 ft.

written.beta: Layback the flake, then the crack for hands overhead, to reach a V-shaped slot guarded by two questionable bolts; stem through it and top out on easy ground.
A long, classic chimney.
Track the line of bolts along the left side of a prominent dark streak.
Climb the chimney; protection and rock quality are both good and the climbing is enjoyable.
written.anchor: Build a belay from gear on top

written.beta: Dramatic laybacking along a flake that opens leftward, followed by more flakes and some jamming, ends at a bolted anchor. A direct start via the neighbouring crack is possible.
A direct line straight up the middle of the face.
Follow the sharp finger-width crack through huecos and multi-coloured rock; solid face holds and excellent protection arrive precisely when needed.
A lovely thin crack that curves up the wall, reached via a scramble over the face just beside the tree on its right.

First pitch: start with gear placed off someone's shoulders or from a stick, aid until it goes free, then trace the crack leftward and up to the fixed belay.

Second pitch: traverse rightward under the big roof until you balance on an iron flake the size of a plate, then crank the obvious roof-capped dihedral crack.
Follow the splitter hand-to-fist crack to its bulging exit moves, then finish by the large cedar tree.
Layback the large flake to the horn on top and then trend rightward to finish.
Follow the line with a central crack; it drifts right near the top, and finishing straight up is the harder variation.
Start at the right side and work leftward, passing a vintage piton plus three bolts that spin, to reach the top.
Follow the wide crack set in a shallow, narrow dihedral, stemming and grinding upward.

Reach to a solid hand jam in the roof crack, then swing your legs up high and into it. Shuffle outward until a flip around is possible, landing on a good stance under a bulge.

Mantle the bulge, then keep climbing wide crack to the top.
Go beyond the lower anchors, over the crux bulge and into steeper stone, finishing at the upper pair of anchors.
Locate a groove at the base for your start, follow it, then straddle the rounded edge to the summit of the pinnacle.

The lower part is a grubby, moderate crack from offwidth to fist size that runs up to a shelf just short of the top. Above, an overhanging fist crack takes the final twenty feet, and a short chimney completes the route.
Squirm up the corner as a chimney. Gear is minimal: one tiny cam or a single stopper fits around a third of the way up.
Begin by following the route before it to the shelf twenty-five feet off the ground, then take the pleasant hand-width split in the face to your right to another ledge.
It shares a face with its neighbour South of Zimbabwe, though past the bolt it angles upward and rightward to horizontal breaks. Get gear in, follow a flake, then pull hard to the top.
Start in the right-hand crack of the pair, then switch left partway and fight a pump onto the ledge.
Climb the offwidth to the perch.

Haul on jugs through a succession of small overhangs with good gear throughout; scramble the small ledges toward the first overhang, then keep following solid holds across four overhangs up to a belay on a large boulder.

From a crack behind a tree on the training wall's right side, ascend 25 feet to a stance near the Sherpa Connection tree, then continue upward beyond another tree, then via the evident break at the main wall's left.

Start near the centre of the pristine white wall beneath a broken thin seam; work the seam to a horizontal crack beneath the first overhang, drift leftward and upward through the tiered overhangs passing a petite triangular beak, grab the bucket at the lip, and mantle onto easier ground.
Begin by the big tree where the ramp starts on the left, and follow the prominent rightward-angling crack all the way up.
Starts from the top of the bouldering wall, with an exposed sidestep at Topaz, then crosses the ledge toward the corner's foot, which the final pitch ascends.
Pitch one aids the vertical crack, which leans out slightly and bulges near the top, up toward the belay spot; most of it is fixed. Pitch two ends along a slim crack.
Face climb for about twenty feet past three bolts, then head leftward into a crack lodged behind the flake. Edge rightward beneath the slanting corner to the lip anchors.
Around the bend left of Wedged, a right-facing corner contains a chimney narrow enough to squeeze. Squirm your way to the pinnacle's summit.
The original way up this spire follows the north-facing front side to the summit.
Get up the right-facing dihedral on the left of its famous neighbor to the ledge, where the hardest move is.

The route follows a steep, loose rib splitting a pair of big drainages. Keep to the rib's crest instead of dropping into the gullies on either side. Expect sections of exposure with big loose blocks, and test every hold. The rib tops out on the west (northwest) summit. From there, traverse the crest to the slightly higher east summit, then continue along the ridge crest before descending the rubbly slopes toward Crater Lake.

South Sister (10,358'): from the Devils Lake Trailhead, climb the South Sister climbers' trail through forest and onto the open plateau, then continue north up the South Ridge on steep scree, skirting the Lewis Glacier's moraine lake on its west side, to the crater rim and around to the summit - a Class 2 walk-up on loose volcanic rock. Leave the summit down the Northwest Ridge (Class 2, snow early and scree late; the Eugene Glacier snowfield lies along its flank) and drop north toward the saddle with Middle Sister above Camp Lake. Middle Sister (10,047'): climb the South Ridge, mostly big talus (Class 2), to the summit, then descend the North Ridge (Class 2-3; it can hold steep snow or ice early in the season) and follow the upper edge of the Collier Glacier to the saddle between Prouty Point and North Sister. North Sister (10,085'): scramble loose slopes onto the South Ridge and follow climbers' paths that alternate between west-side ledges and the east side at gaps. Below the summit pinnacle, cross the Terrible Traverse - a steep, exposed snowfield with a nasty runout in early and mid-summer, an easy Class 3 scree crossing once melted out - then turn up into the Bowling Alley, a steep, loose gully between the pinnacle's horns. Its headwall is easy but loose Class 4; above it, Class 2-3 leads to the summit block.

First pitch: follow solid holds up a series of corners onto a ramp that slants rightward, and stop beside Fatman Flake, under a steeper headwall, to belay.

Second pitch: go up the flake, veer leftward onto a ledge, then keep climbing easy rock where no gear is available, or move left to belay at the summit.
Hand-jamming on sound rock gives way to lower-angled ground.

Begin from a little detached block at the face's left, trend upward and rightward, clipping a bolt on the way to a tiny overlap (a good gear spot), then keep going directly upward by two further bolts to a flake and gentler slab finishing.
Layback the wide crack in the dominant inside corner to anchors by the left wall.
Start in a slender crack that kinks sharply leftward about ten feet up, work it until a decent horizontal hold, then finish on easier ground.
From the balcony shelf, follow the evident crack running up the upper wall's centre.

Climb a short crack of about fifteen feet to a comfortable ledge at the foot of the main corner and belay there.

Then climb the huge corner above.
Ascend the slab beside the ledge's left end, clipping a pair of bolts en route to a flake; stay on the flake, clip one further bolt and set up the belay on slings.

Start as Thar She Blows does but bear right straight away to the evident flake, climb it to the horizontal break, then follow that break far across to the right until slab climbing takes you to the top.

Grade IV, WI3 Moderate Snow. Steep hourglass rock/ice section (40-50 ft), ~45° snow slope, 5th class rock band, ~4,000 ft of climbing from the bivy to Liberty Cap. Rockfall hazard (climb early). Crevasses, avalanche debris. Two-day approach recommended. Best June-August.

bivy.name: Lower Ptarmigan Ridge camp
bivy.notes: Bivy ground on lower Ptarmigan Ridge above Spray Park, from which parties drop onto the North Mowich Glacier. Mowich Lake has had no road access since the Fairfax Bridge on SR 165 closed in 2025, so check access first.
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier wilderness permit and climbing registration
bivy.capacity: A few tent sites on rock and snow

bivy.name: High bivy between the North Mowich and Edmunds glaciers
bivy.notes: The usual bivouac before the headwall, on the divide between the two glaciers.

written.beta: Eight pitches of flakes and cracks of all sizes — including a fun roof-pull/lieback P1, a finger-crack P2, a steep lichen-covered finger-crack crux P3 (5.10c), 4th-class terrain, a fun chimney P5, a poor-rock corner P6, a heads-up, minimal-gear P7 (5.10), and rambling 5.7 terrain to the summit — make for a varied, tough outing that tests route-finding as much as climbing.

Climbs the southeast ridge in about eight pitches up to 5.6 to the southeast spire, a false summit and the lowest of Argonaut's three summits, then carries on to the true summit on the west spire. The lower pitches are blocky and awkward, carry a lot of lichen and are somewhat hard to protect. The line includes two single-rope rappels, or one double-rope rappel, into the notch. The main summit needs a short, non-exposed Class 4 move to its highest block after Class 3 ridge traversing.
written.approach: Start at the Beverly Turnpike Trailhead at the end of FR-9737-112 (roughly 3,650 ft). At about 0.5 mile, bear left onto signed Trail #1391 (Beverly Turnpike/Beverly Creek Trail) — do not miss this junction, as a wrong-fork error onto the Bean Creek Trail is a commonly reported mistake. Continue to roughly 3.1 miles and turn right onto Trail #1226.1 (Fourth Creek Trail), climbing to Fourth Creek Pass at about 3.6 miles (roughly 5,900-6,000 ft), which opens up the first real views of Argonaut, Colchuck, and Dragontail. From the pass, descend the well-maintained trail on the far side to the south shore of Ingalls Creek at about 6 miles (roughly 4,200-4,250 ft); ford the creek (wading or a footlog depending on the season/year) to reach flat camping at the Fourth Creek/Ingalls Creek confluence. From camp, leave the Ingalls Creek Trail and climb generally north into the gentle, heather-and-slab Porcupine Creek drainage on Argonaut's south side, working up open basin terrain beside the southeast ridge, the crest that rises from this side to the southeast spire. The roped climbing follows that crest, about eight pitches to the southeast spire. Hazards: the Ingalls Creek ford can be a real obstacle in early season or after rain; the basin approach involves loose talus and, in shoulder season, hard snow that may warrant an axe and crampons; this is a long, remote approach (partial day just to reach the base) so plan for a car-camp or bivy. A second way in comes from Colchuck Lake over the Argonaut-Colchuck col. On the Ingalls Creek side the trails are easy to follow, but the off-trail climb above the creek is a tough bushwhack.

written.beta: Predominantly bolted with mixed trad protection. South-facing provides good sun exposure.

The route involves four major vertical steps. The lower approach consists of approximately 2,300 feet of brush fighting up steep cliffs through dense vegetation (slide alder, vine maple, devil's club). The climbing involves vertical, delicate mixed terrain with roof sections requiring stirrup aid climbing on unusually hard rock (no specific rock type has been reliably sourced for this face) with poor natural protection. The crux is on the second step (400 feet) which features 120-degree roof sections and extremely delicate vertical climbing. On the lower brush sections, the first-ascent party fixed hundreds of feet of light ¼-inch rope hung from the brush to assist with load-hauling, with separate lengths of full-diameter climbing rope fixed at the most hazardous spots; double fixed ropes were placed specifically on the first step for hauling loads. Multiple attempts from 1951-1959 failed before the successful first ascent in 1960.

bivy.name: Barclay Lake
bivy.notes: This is the one genuinely established camp in the zone and the obvious base for the Barclay Creek peaks. It sits at 2,420 ft in a narrow trench with Baring Mountain's north face rising straight out of the south shore and Merchant Peak and Gunn Peak on the north side, so nearly every objective on that road starts from here or from the road below it. Two miles and about 200 ft of net gain from the trailhead, which makes it a realistic place to sleep the night before rather than a committing carry. From the east end of the lake, boot paths climb north to Stone and Eagle Lakes and give the standard way onto Merchant and Gunnshy. Note that Baring's north face and Dolomite Tower are reached by leaving the trail and grinding up the south side of the valley — brushy, loose, and a different proposition from the walk to the lake. Realistically most parties here climb car-to-car and use this camp only if they want a pre-dawn start without the two-hour drive, or if they got benighted and walked out late. One current caveat: the footlog over Barclay Creek on the approach has been removed for safety and a replacement has no date, so plan on a ford or a log-hop and expect that to be genuinely awkward during spring runoff.
bivy.water: The lake and Barclay Creek run all year. Treat everything; this is a heavily used shoreline. In hard winter the lake freezes and the creek runs under snow.
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit. The trail corridor and the lake itself were deliberately left OUT of the Wild Sky Wilderness so that larger groups could keep using them, so the twelve-person wilderness party limit does not apply at the lake — but it does apply the moment you leave the corridor onto any of these peaks. Parking at the trailhead takes a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass, or a day fee; a Washington Discover Pass is not valid. Check the current forest-wide campfire ban before planning a fire, and camp only in the existing sites.
bivy.capacity: Several established lakeside sites strung along the north shore, plus a few set back in the trees. Popular, and full most summer weekends — it is one of the easiest overnight walks on this stretch of highway. Two vault toilets serve the lake.

bivy.name: Dolomite Camp
bivy.notes: Camp at the base of the first of the four vertical steps, after the brush-fighting approach.

written.beta: From a camp near Dutch Miller Gap, ascend the left-hand of two parallel gullies on the SW Face (~1,000 ft, Class 3-4) to a ridge notch NW of the true summit, then climb the summit block in three short pitches (up to 5.6) to the top.

The standard approach ascends unroped via ledges on the east/southeast face to minimize rockfall danger. Parties typically establish camps at Boston Basin low camp (5,300 ft) or high camp (6,400 ft), then traverse via the Boston-Sahale saddle to access the summit route. Most ascents run roughly 10-11 hours from high camp to summit and back, per the detailed schedule.

This is considered the standard and easiest route up Burgundy Spire. Recommended for climbers experienced in alpine rock and comfortable with route-finding on exposed terrain. The route features many traverses, down-climbs, and loose features that demand careful attention.

This is one of the two main routes on Cannon Mountain and is recommended only as an ascent route. It's best done in mid-to-late summer once snow has melted from around Coney Lake and off the ridge. The route starts at the Stuart Lake Trailhead, climbs steep, bushy, loose burned slopes to the ridge crest, then follows and traverses below the crest -- including a notorious 0.3-mile loose traverse below a band of towers that can't be climbed directly -- before a talus gully and short final scramble to the summit block.
A 5.7 trad route in The Castle's climbing area alongside the easy-5th-class Southeast Face; no detailed pitch-by-pitch description, approach specifics, or first-ascent history is on record.

Established in 1989, this is the second-best-known line on Chianti's east face and a quieter alternative to Rebel Yell at a full grade easier. It starts directly below the summit, following a long left-leaning ramp up into a left-facing corner and an off-width crack; three more pitches cross Rebel Yell and gain the notch between Burgundy Spire and Chianti, and a short pitch reaches the summit up the normal route. It is graded II 5.9 or III 5.9. Detail is thin: pitch lengths and total footage are not known, so this is a route for a party comfortable route-finding on an alpine face rather than following a topo.

From the upper Chimney Glacier, cross the moat at the foot of the rock and climb the face to the left of the main gully that drops from the notch between the central and south summits. About three pitches of wet, slippery fourth-class ground lead to a system of ledges, some of them very wide, that runs up to just below the notch, roughly 600 vertical ft above the glacier. From the notch, climb about 400 ft more to the South Peak.

From the far side of Colchuck Lake, hike uphill to gain the moraine, follow it to the right, and drop into the large couloir at the edge of the Colchuck Glacier. In winter and early season it is continuous snow the entire way; later in summer, Class 4 rock can be exposed in a few short steps. The route can be climbed minimalist and fast, or fully protected with rock gear, pickets, and screws.

Follow the couloir off the Colchuck Glacier as it winds upward and steepens; the gully hits a steep wall, so continue along the base of this wall to climber's left to find the exit, finishing on steep snow/ice to 60+ degrees that gains the summit ridge. It is usually rated roughly Grade II with an elevation gain of about 1,500 ft from the glacier to the ridge; some grade it up to Grade III depending on conditions.

West Ridge via the Colonial Glacier. From the Pyramid Lake Trailhead on SR-20, follow the trail to Pyramid Lake, then a steep climbers' path up the forested rib to camps near the edge of the Colonial Glacier (~6,000 ft). Cross the glacier toward the Colonial-Snowfield col, gain the west ridge through a notch, and follow the exposed ridge (class 3-4 with short low-5th steps) to the summit; many parties rappel the summit block on descent. Crevasse hazard on the glacier; loose rock and exposure on the ridge. Best July-September. No confirmed public GPS track for this route; navigation skills required.
written.detailed_rack: Glacier travel kit (rope, pickets/screws as conditions dictate) plus a few small-to-mid cams/nuts and slings for the short class 4 summit step and the optional horn rappel; a 30m single rope is plenty. Ice axe, crampons, rope and glacier travel kit.

written.beta: From the Alpental base area, ascend barren lower slopes to snowline, then follow the Lower International run and the steep, double-black-diamond Upper International run. From the top of Upper International, a wide ramp leads to a clump of alpine fir below the summit block; a steel cable protects a down-sloping, exposed rock-ledge traverse, followed by a short Class 2-3 scramble to the summit, which carries a radio tower and marker pole.
From below the E side of the formation, work up a series of zig-zagging ledges to the summit; a short 4th-class perfect hand-crack section is one of the standard variations.

Traverse right from start toward the large hanging 'split block'. Pitch 1 offers a 5.8 finger crack or easier ground to its right, and pitch 2 has a critical 25-30 foot unprotectable section on a dyke. Pitch 3 climbs through a chimney and dirty corner. The final pitch offers laid-back climbing in an obvious corner approach to summit, though the final moves to the horned summit are unprotectable. The route requires careful rock quality assessment and awareness of unprotected sections.

The South Route climbs East Twin Needle from Crescent Creek Basin by the loose south-facing gullies to the Eye Col, the notch between East and West Twin Needle. Small chockstones low in the gully are scrambled past; the larger ones higher up are fifth class and are usually pitched, and a short scree walk finishes at the col. From the col the route climbs the steep summit block directly above, with a short hand-crack crux near the top that can hold ice early in the season; the summit is small, with a sheer drop to the east. This is a different climb from the hard southeast ridge/face (east arête) put up during the 2003 Southern Pickets enchainment, which is reached along the crest from the east and is not gained from the Eye Col.

Climbed via the historic 1945 Beckey-Staley line on the spire's southeast side: from the east notch, a short pitch gains a ramp system that is followed up and west, then a final slab/crack pitch (crux) leads to a summit ledge. The rock is loose in places (especially early in a pitch or on the east aspect), so care with hand/footholds and rope management is important on this wandering line.

Despite the peak's craggy appearance suggesting no easy line exists, erosion has cut a class 3 gully/weakness up the west side that is catalogued as a named, rated route (skill 2 / fitness 2). It tops out on a summit divided into two high points roughly 100 ft apart — the north summit is slightly higher, and the south summit has notably more exposure, with a steep slab dropping toward the East Face.

The standard route leaves the trail system at Bird Creek Camp (4,200 ft) on the Devore Creek Trail and goes cross-country: through open forest and meadow to a saddle just south of Enigma Peak (~6,400 ft), down a scree gully to cross upper Castle Creek, then up Flora's southwest ridge on talus and scree to the summit. It is rated the least difficult of the Stehekin-area 'Top 100' peaks (compare neighboring Devore, Tupshin, and Riddle) and requires no rope, rack, or technical rock climbing — just sturdy boots, off-trail navigation, and tolerance for loose rock. The peak's namesake first ascent (Leuthold/Metzger, 1940) is attested for the mountain overall, but no published account gives it used this specific southwest line, so it is not attributed to the route here.
written.approach: From Chelan, take the Lady of the Lake ferry (or a floatplane) to Stehekin Landing. Ride the NPS shuttle bus 4.4 miles up Stehekin Valley Road to Harlequin Bridge ($5 fare), cross the bridge, and follow the road past Harlequin Camp and the Stehekin Airport to pick up the Stehekin River Trail. Follow this mostly flat trail southeastward about 3 miles to the signed Devore Creek Trail junction. The Devore Creek Trail then climbs steeply through rock bluffs and open forest for about 1 mile, enters the Glacier Peak Wilderness, and traverses brushy, dry hillside for roughly 3 more miles to Bird Creek Camp (4,200 ft) — the only designated camp in the area, with room for about three tents. From Bird Creek Camp, most parties do Flora as a long day round trip: bushwhack through open forest (spiderwebs, chest-high brush, and blowdown reported) toward the saddle south of Enigma Peak, then follow the route description above to the summit. A longer alternate approach reaches the same southwest slope and west cirque from Holden Village via Railroad Creek Road and Tenmile Pass; it is used mainly by parties combining Flora with Riddle Peak and Black Tower.

written.beta: From the East Ridge saddle beside the Solitary Gendarme, downclimb the dirty gully on the north side for roughly 100 ft and exit left (northwest) onto the ledges - going lower runs into cliffs. Traverse northwest across roughly five rock ribs on sandy, grassy ledges and down-sloping slabs, mostly 3rd class with short 4th-class moves at each rib, staying close to the level at which the gully was left: too low meets the cliffs above the Boston Glacier, too high the steeper, corrugated ribs. Cairns mark the easiest line across most rib crossings (a higher and lower cairn at each rib). Where the North Ridge stops the traverse, climb the small northeast face below the summit: 3rd-class ledges, a short grassy traverse west to the next rib, then steepening Class 4 to the summit rocks. The face is lined with slung rappel stations that can double as belays; many parties belay the upper part. Allow about 2 hours from the saddle to the summit, more if belaying.

bivy.name: Glade Saddle
bivy.notes: A tight, well-used two-person bivy site at the saddle above the razorback.

written.beta: Climb the glacier (now largely a series of persistent snowfields rather than a crevassed glacier) near the center of the cirque, right of the rock band that splits the upper and lower sections, then right of the snow dome to gain the ridge. A rough goat and boot path on the usually snow-free southwest side leads to a small saddle just east of the true summit, and a short, loose class 3 scramble finishes it. Popular and the most straightforward line up the peak, though it is a long outing (~20 miles round trip) with real elevation gain.
Short scramble up to a belay area, then a brief but engaging climb; the crux is moving up onto a ledge right before the anchor, with a view toward Mt. Rainier in the distance.
written.location: Just past the first set of bolts on the adjacent route Enchanting Puller Blind (5.10c)

written.beta: Climbs the big, blocky groove between Just Enough and Notta Slab. Shares its start with Notta Slab, then breaks left into a wide, chimney-like feature after the 2nd bolt. 16 bolts to chain anchors.
written.location: Big blocky groove between Just Enough and Notta Slab

written.beta: Serious alpine scramble requiring climbing experience and high mountain skills. Technical crux is an exposed class 3-4 hidden ramp with loose rock and significant exposure. A narrow ledge on north side of summit requires careful foot placement, especially in wet or icy conditions. Multiple search and rescue incidents have occurred on this peak.

Scramble ~200 feet of loose, mossy, dirty slabs to reach first anchor. Climb 6 pitches of mixed alpine rock through crumbly terrain to Lunch Ledge at ~300 feet. The iconic traverse (pitches 4-5) traverses right on good ledges with old fixed pitons; now requires careful downclimbing due to 2021 damage. Upper pitches climb Class 4 ramp terrain with trees and exposure to summit. Route is sustained and exposed throughout; not a beginner alpine rock climb.

Ascend a very large ramp that traverses the entire face from north to south. The climbing starts up a steep crack/face (crux) for approximately 30 feet of low 5th class, then transitions to Class 4 for about half a rope length through rocks and alpine trees with exposure. Climbing continues via mixed scrambling and rock sections to the summit. Route involves significant high-consequence scrambling.

From a large clearing around 4000-4200 ft, climb to the saddle between Cave Ridge and Guye Peak, then turn right (south) and follow the ridge to Guye's north summit — class 3 in summer. The 'Hidden Ridge' variation continues from the north summit around an outcropping to a hidden ridge with one 5.4 move (otherwise class 4), rappelling ~30 ft off a slung horn to the notch between the north and middle summits; this was found to be a more direct, more enjoyable line than the standard gully descent in winter/spring conditions.
The last push is Class 2 with a short Class 3 step, climbing loose scree and talus to the summit; exposure is generally minimal for experienced parties.
written.approach: From Glacier, WA, drive Mt. Baker Highway (SR 542) east about 1 mile past the Glacier Public Service Center to Glacier Creek Road (FS 39); turn right, then take an immediate left onto Deadhorse Road (FS 37). FS 37 normally continues 12.7 miles to the Skyline Divide Trailhead. FS 37 has been closed by the 2021 flood washout at milepost 3.1, and during the repair work it is gated near its start (mile 0.03), so the trailhead is not reachable by vehicle; check the road's status before planning around it. When open, hike Skyline Divide Trail #678 through old-growth forest switchbacks and into meadows on the ridge crest (~2 mi), follow the crest to the trail's high point (~6,563 ft, ~4.5 mi), then continue cross-country along the open ridge to Chowder Ridge and the base of Hadley Peak. Past the high point the maintained tread fades into a boot-packed path that follows the open ridge crest for roughly another 3 miles, over minor ups and downs on Chowder Ridge, to the base of the final scramble.

written.beta: A boot path for Hibox leaves the main trail here (or at the second chute crossing) and climbs steeply but stays class 2 through timber to near treeline. Above the trees, go right around the first band of cliffs, then left around a rock outcrop, continue through more timber to a second cliff band, and take the gully on the right to gain the upper mountain. From there head right (east) along the south side of the summit rocks to a gully on the east side, which is climbed with a bit of class 3 near the top to reach the summit. Route-finding is the main challenge; there is no continuous trail above the boot path.

written.anchor: Chain anchor at the top of the cliff

written.beta: From Sahale Glacier Camp (or a Horseshoe Basin camp), cross into Horseshoe Basin, gain the base of a class 3 dike/gully system below Ripsaw Ridge, and follow it (with a short class 4 step) up to the ridge crest near the 'Lick of Flame' spire. From there a narrow ramp leads to the summit; it begins as 3rd-class terrain and turns into a short section of 5th-class (5.2) climbing in its final ~100 ft below the top. Rope up for this last section — most parties treat it as one roughly 100-ft pitch.
Face climbing builds to a constriction (crux) and small roof with great holds; hard sections can be bypassed. Sits in the shade all day with excellent views from the anchors.
written.location: West side, left of a large overhanging feature

written.beta: The lower northeast ridge section climbs 4th-to-easy-fifth-class (5.4 max) slabs and cracks on excellent rock. It's followed by the crux upper east-face pitch, graded 5.6 X on rock described as horrible, with almost no protection - this is not a route for the average 5.6 climber, and picking the wrong line on the face can be fatal.

Begins with juggy holds and progresses through increasingly technical movement. The crux comes right before the last bolt, with an option to move right or take a recently-cleaned left-side slot finish.
written.anchor: Anchor 6 ft above the final bolt, partly hidden behind small trees

written.beta: This is an early-season snow climb, done when the north cirque is still filled in. The Nohokomeen Glacier runs from about 6,100 ft to 8,200 ft, is over 340 acres, and is heavily crevassed after the midpoint of its descent, so rope up. Above the glacier the headwall is the crux: it is variously described as 700 vertical feet of snow at slopes up to 60 degrees, and as a sustained 50-55 degrees for about 800 feet with steeper steps. Most parties simul-climb it, taking turns kicking steps, with a rope over the shoulder for the bergschrund; winter parties have pitched it out with pickets, cams, nuts and screws through a mixed cliff band. The bergschrund is the main obstacle and normally goes on a single bridge on the left side. Above, exit onto the ridge and finish along a narrow, corniced summit ridge with rocky drops — the last few hundred feet are the most exposed of the route.

Kololo Peaks presents three viable multi-day approaches, all exceeding 12 miles and typically requiring 2-3 days with glacier travel. The climb itself is straightforward Class 2-3 scrambling on talus and snow, with the primary challenge being glacier crevasse navigation and length of approach rather than technical difficulty. Neither summit presents hard climbing; the route involves walking across easy terrain between the west summit and the slightly higher east summit (8,240 ft, the true high point).

Start on low-angle dihedral left of Lexington-Minuteman gully. Ascend via cracks and chimneys; crux is pitch 5 with exposed traverse. Upper pitches are off-width and chimney climbing. Standard trad rack essential; doubles to #3 plus a #4, with a single #5 or #6 useful for the short wide sections.

Grade III alpine rock, 5.11 crux. Four pitches on Liberty Bell West Face. Pitch 1 (5.8): Slab moves left into corner with short bulge. Pitch 2 (5.11 crux): Steep, awkward fist crack past the right side of a roof, physical, excellent gear. Pitch 3 (5.10): Left-angling hand crack with roof/bulge exit. Pitch 4 (5.7): Navigate tunnel or harder left slab variation, then simul/scramble on exposed sunny arete to summit. Excellent hand crack climbing with minimal traffic. Hazards: loose rock from freeze-thaw cycles, afternoon thunderstorms, exposure on final arete.

Grade: 5.12 (YDS), Grade IV overall. 11 pitches, approximately 1,100 feet of climbing. Route follows intricate crack systems and faces on East Face of Liberty Bell. Hazards: significant rock fall danger in approach gully (parties above knock rock down it, bowling-alley style); loose rock throughout approach; exposed alpine terrain; weather exposure on big wall. Required skills: advanced alpine rock climbing, 5.11+ crack climbing, self-rescue, anchor building, multi-pitch experience. First ascent: 1967 (aid climbing); free ascent variation established 2008 by Mikey Schaefer. Best season: June-September; July-September strongly preferred (late June requires ice axe, crampons). Notable: route features substantial fixed gear on most pitches.

Start on the northwest face just right of the prominent hanging glacier with a 60 m WI4 pitch, the route's crux, shared with Shooting Gallery on neighbouring Assassin Spire; its upper half is overhanging, poorly protected ice of doubtful quality. Above, cross a snowfield and climb a vertical ice curtain and a well-protected step of glacial ice into the upper amphitheater, the basin between Lincoln Peak and Assassin Spire, simul-climbing along its west side. On Lincoln's northwest wall, about four roped pitches of steeper ice follow, with snowfields up to 70° between them; the obvious central flow gives about 120 m of WI3+ in two long pitches. From the upper snowfield, follow a rime-covered ridge to a sub-summit, downclimb a short rime step, and climb a final icy gully to the summit.

The historic standard route on Lincoln Peak; the only other line is a rarely formed northwest-face ice route. Technical snow and ice climbing with significant avalanche risk. Route comprises multiple sections: 30-40 degree initial snowfields, crux serac obstacle requiring 70-85 degree ice climbing (50 feet high), hidden gully with 2-4 foot deep runnels, narrow exposed snow aretes with steep drop-offs, and final 50-degree gully to summit rocks. Climb early morning when snow is frozen; conditions deteriorate rapidly with afternoon warming.

From the pass, head roughly south-southwest past Isolation and Tranquil Lakes toward Little Annapurna's northeast ridge, then follow cairns up open granite slabs and talus on the peak's north side to the summit -- one of three rocky high points on the ridge, with the true summit being the middle one. The line itself involves minimal exposure and only occasional Class 3 moves, but Aasgard Pass is the physical and route-finding crux of the day.
The summit push itself is straightforward (class 3) once you're on site; the real crux of the route is the multi-day glacier approach to get there.

From Luna Cirque, climb steepening glacier/snow up the hanging glacier below the peak (the technical crux, and reportedly impassable late in the season) to a notch, then transition to rock. Two to three pitches of easy 5th-class slab climbing lead up to the summit ridge; stay off the towers on the south side and climb the final 25-ft summit block directly.

Ascend easy slopes southwest of Magic Mountain to the base of the ridge/face. Climb steep rock and finally an easy chimney to a notch northwest of the summit (the same notch reached by the North Face route), then traverse and climb the short remaining distance to the summit via the NW face.
Climb any of the heathery gullies at the north or northeast head of the cirque to gain the summit ridge, then finish to the top.

From the lake, gain the ridge above and continue cross-country toward the summit, bypassing a false summit before reaching the true top. The line is difficult to follow, brushy, and has claimed parties onto unwanted 4th-class terrain when off-route; a Aug-2024 trip report logged 14.75 miles round trip, about 5,400' of gain, and 7 hours car-to-car via a non-standard east-ridge/south-ridge variant, noting the descent line is easy to lose.

Excellent, solid rock, an outstanding summit position, and a quick, easy approach/descent have made this the area's most-climbed line (250+ logged ascents). Grades run 5.8-5.10a across 7 pitches on the crest of the pillar.
A straightforward snow/ice route up to 50°, following the northwest face of the North Ridge.
written.detailed_rack: A snow picket, at least one ice screw, and a few thin pitons. A snow picket, an ice screw, possibly a few thin pins, and two ice tools.

written.beta: The most popular and easiest way up the mountain. From the South Climb/Cold Springs trailhead the route follows an old roadbed through the 2012 Cascade Creek burn scar, climbs into subalpine meadows, crosses the Round-the-Mountain Trail and the PCT, then ascends Crescent Ridge to broad snowfields leading past Lunch Counter to Piker's Peak and the true summit.
written.detailed_rack: No technical protection is used on the standard line; rope and glacier gear are not needed. Ice axe and crampons; no rope or technical protection on the standard line in normal conditions.

written.beta: The summer line follows the crest from the 4,900-ft saddle over Peak 5681; the usual snow-season line differs: near the Lake Ann junction, leave the trail and work up heather benches and talus, staying fairly high on the east side of Mount Annette (nicknamed 'Little Ann') rather than dropping into brush, then continue up a gully (often snow-filled and roughly following a fault line) to gain the summit ridge and the top of Mount Ann. The off-trail portion is generally straightforward Class 2 route-finding, though boot paths can peter out higher up and steeper sections may warrant an ice-axe self-belay. Reported round-trip stats vary by GPS track/route taken (10.5 mi RT / 4,000 ft gain is the commonly listed figure; individual logs have recorded figures as low as ~11 mi / ~3,400 ft), reflecting that this is an off-trail line rather than a fixed path.

It crosses the lower Boulder Glacier northwest to the base of the cleaver (~6,800 ft), following the cleaver as the climbing steepens, becomes icy, and grows exposed to rockfall near crevasses, before joining the upper mountain near the Boulder Glacier's summit approach.

Grade: 4th class YDS, AI2-3 ice, M1b mixed, PG-13. Technical: 3,000 ft vertical gain over 5 pitches on the ridge itself. Hazards: Extremely loose and unstable rock (especially late season), bergschrunds, extensive crevassing, icefall terrain. Route: From the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead, cross Coleman and Roosevelt Glaciers northeastward, climb low-moderate snow ramps to ridge at ~7,500 ft, bypass Cockscomb Tower on left via steep snow, continue ridge to summit. Required: Ice climbing competency, crevasse rescue skills, glacier travel experience, rock scrambling ability. Best season: Spring or early summer (late season loose rock creates high hazard). First ascent: July 4, 1961 (Murley, Musser, Vielbig).
The glacier itself is moderately angled with one steeper section on the Roman Wall just below the summit plateau.

Mount Ballard's south side is a Class 3 scramble from a camp at the old Azurite Mine on Mill Creek. Above camp the climb is steep, rocky ground with two cruxes: a band of brush low on the mountain and, higher up, picking the gully that actually leads to the summit block, where a few short steps need hands. The higher of Ballard's two summits is the southern one. The east ridge from the Slate Creek side is a separate, harder line described under its own approach.

The standard (and only non-technical) line on Buckindy climbs class 4 terrain on the north slopes, close by glacier remnants on the mountain's north and east flanks. Separate class 5 rock climbing exists on the southwest-facing 'Buckindy Crags,' outside the scope of this standard scramble route.

The route gains the glacier via Easy Ridge or Wiley Ridge, then traverses moderate snowfields, crosses a bergschrund, and finishes with a Class 5 rock pitch on the summit horn. Fixed anchors exist for protection and rappels. The route sees relatively stable conditions July through early September; later season snowbridge degradation can make the bergshrund impassable.

This is a remote, multi-day approach-plus-climb rather than a roadside route. Crampons and axe are used on the couloir to a north-ridge saddle (~5,600 ft), then the route dips down to and ropes up across the Christie Glacier (steep enough in places that parties rope up even without visible crevasses). A high col just left (east) of the true summit has been reported as unexpectedly difficult — a chossy, eroded, sometimes-overhanging short cliff with a rotten, exposed ledge traverse (class 4) — harder than it used to be, with at least one large rockfall changing the crux between recent seasons. Above the col, dense krummholz gives way to the southeast summit ridge for class 2-3 scrambling to the top.

From Upper Royal Basin, ascend heather/talus to the moraine rim, drop to snowfields and climb to the ~6,900 ft col between Clark and Mount Johnson. From the col, ascend talus to the cliff base and skirt right on a wide, low-angle (Class 2) southwest-facing ledge — exposed-looking but easy. Where the cliffs split into a Y-shaped gully, go straight up to a boulder then right to a notch on the SE ridge (Class 2-3), descend the ridge to an east ledge via a diagonal crack system (Class 3, exposed but solid), follow the ledge north, then climb a loose gully (Class 3) to a dihedral ramp (Class 4, or a Class 3 broken face alternative on the left) and finally a shallow slot through the north face of the summit block (Class 3-4, good holds). Route-finding is the main difficulty; published descriptions are described by multiple parties as sketchy, and several climbers have produced their own route sketches after the fact.
Once through the approach, the SW Flank itself is a moderate 3rd/4th-class scramble on open slopes and ledges to the summit — no technical rock climbing required.

This is the most frequently ascended route. Start from Ouzel Lake (~5,700 ft) and head eastward up the west slopes, which are semi-open initially and transition to alpine terrain around 6,200 ft. Minor cliffbands require Class 3 scrambling to navigate around. Climb to the obvious SW basin (~7,700 ft), continue to the 8,260-ft notch immediately south of the summit, then traverse the final chossy South Ridge to the summit. The peak is known for exceptionally loose, fractured volcanic rock throughout.

From the upper trailhead the trail climbs almost immediately via stacked switchbacks for about 0.3 mile before merging with the longer lower-trailhead trail at roughly 3,900 ft. From there it continues at a steady, 'character-building' grade through forest, breaks out of the trees into rock-strewn slopes and gravelly meadows, passes through a notch, and finishes with a short scramble to the true summit. It is a non-technical trail/scramble (no rope or rack needed in summer conditions) but is consistently steep with minimal flat ground. This is the standard, most direct route.

Mount Fairchild is the second-highest peak in the Bailey Range. Both ways in involve significant glacier travel with crevasse hazards and require proper alpine mountaineering skills. The peak stands at the head of Fairchild Creek with the Fairchild Glacier on its east slope.
written.approach: There is no trail to Mount Fairchild itself, but the standard approach follows a well-defined maintained-trail corridor before turning to off-trail wilderness travel. Start at the Sol Duc River Trailhead (end of Sol Duc Road) on the Sol Duc River Trail. At 0.8 mi pass Sol Duc Falls, and at 0.9 mi reach the Lovers Lane junction; branch left onto the Deer Lake Trail, which climbs steeply and relentlessly through switchbacks to Deer Lake (3.4 mi, ~3,527 ft) — the first reliable water and the last easy camping before things get serious. Beyond Deer Lake the trail continues up through Potholes Meadows (~5 mi) and gains the High Divide ridge crest around 6 mi/4,730 ft, with good views and intermittent tarns/snowmelt for water. At 7.4 mi pass the Seven Lakes Basin junction (4,900 ft) — a good last water/camp option — then continue along High Divide past or near Bogachiel Peak (5,474 ft). At roughly 10.2 mi, leave the maintained trail system at the Cat Basin junction; from here it is off-trail cross-country and boot-path travel only, dropping into Cat Basin below Cat Peak (5,940 ft) and then crossing the Catwalk, the narrow, exposed class 3 ridge linking Cat Peak to Mount Carrie (6,995 ft). Past it, many parties use the exposed, loose-talus sidehill traverse across Carrie's south face; an alternative preferred by some climbers is to stay higher on Carrie's north side, which avoids the worst sidehilling and leads up Carrie's ridge and upper flanks to its summit. The route to Fairchild starts from Mount Carrie's summit: head northeast down the Carrie Glacier (rope up and put on crampons here; ice axe mandatory most of the season), circle around to the north of Fairchild, and climb its Southwest Ridge to the 6,899 ft summit. This final section is only thinly described, so expect to find the line yourself. One-way distance to this point is roughly 12 miles with substantial cumulative gain from repeated up-and-down over Bogachiel Peak, Cat Peak, and the Carrie ridge system, consistent with the ~8,000 ft round-trip gain. Hazards: early-season creek crossings near Sol Duc Falls, steep loose-scree switchbacks on the Deer Lake Trail, serious exposure and loose rock on the Catwalk traverse, crevasses and snow bridges on the Carrie Glacier requiring roped glacier travel (especially early/mid-summer), no reliable water between Cat Basin and the glacier, and heavy route-finding demands in fog/whiteout since the entire Cat Basin-to-summit section is unmarked wilderness travel. In late July the glacier east of Mount Carrie can be skirted along its northwest edge on rock; drop to a tarn near 5,900 ft, hold that height to a gully that rises straight to the ridge, then walk the ridge to the top. A second way in leaves from the Elwha River and crosses over Mount Fitzhenry, instead of using the High Divide approach via Sol Duc and Mount Carrie.

written.beta: The route generally follows the south/southwest ridge to the summit over a mix of dirt, talus, and short class 3 rock steps; in early season the ridge and gullies hold snow and are often climbed with an ice axe and crampons, or skied/split-boarded as a ski-mountaineering tour. It is also frequently combined with a loop past Chain Lakes.

This is not a technical climb but a serious backcountry scramble: about 13.1 trail miles from the Staircase trailhead to First Divide/Home Sweet Home camp, then off-trail travel east over talus, heather benches, and a short rocky ridge to the summit.
written.approach: The North Fork Skokomish Trail from Staircase to First Divide and the Home Sweet Home Trail from First Divide down to the Duckabush have been closed since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, with no reopening date; check the park's trail conditions before planning. When open, the standard way in starts at the Staircase trailhead (~785 ft) and follows the North Fork Skokomish River Trail up the valley through old-growth forest, past Camp Pleasant to Nine Stream Camp, where the trail fords the river (deep and swift in high snowmelt or heavy rain). Above Nine Stream it climbs steeply past Two Bear Camp, brushy between Two Bear and the divide, to First Divide (4,688 ft), about 12.5 miles from the trailhead. The much longer alternative comes up the Duckabush River Trail and climbs over First Divide from the north past Home Sweet Home. Just below First Divide on the Skokomish side, the long-abandoned Mount Hopper Way leaves the main trail; its tread has gone under brush, so expect to bushwhack south and east through forest, then climb open talus and subalpine meadow toward Mount Hopper's basin below the summit rockwall (high point ~6,120 ft). This upper stretch has real route-finding difficulty: numerous gullies and ribs look equally plausible from below, snow can choke the gully well into summer (ice axe advisable), and the final scramble features loose rock underfoot — expect to backtrack if you pick the wrong line. Most parties make it a multi-day trip, camping at Two Bear Camp, First Divide or Home Sweet Home rather than pushing car-to-car. A shorter but steeper off-trail alternative starts at Lake of the Angels, reached by the Putvin Trail: cross the ridge, drop into the valley below Mount Stone, then climb the ridge west of Stone toward Hopper.

written.beta: From Crescent Lake's NE side, ascend north up open talus and meadow slopes; the upper mountain narrows into a loose, dirty class 3 gully before easing back to talus and a climbers' trail to the summit. Many parties combine the ascent with a traverse to neighboring Mount Mastiff (about 1 mile away) or Rock Mountain for a full Nason Ridge outing.

written.detailed_rack: Use the full length of a 70m rope if rappelling on a single rope, which is recommended. Bring 16 draws, 2-4 of them alpine. All anchors are bolted and set up for rappel. A stick clip for the headwall bolts.

written.beta: Locate the gully system in the rocky face with two narrow channels 30 feet apart; take the right channel and ascend the narrow then open gully to broken rock to attain the ridge top. Follow the ridge, favoring the west side, to the summit. Most of ridge top has a way trail and the route is partially marked with cairns after leaving the basin, but cairns may be far apart and the way trail may disappear for long stretches. If you lose cairns or way trail most gullies probably work though some may be more difficult than others.

From Flapjack Lakes, either contour around to the right or climb east and then south over the forested ridge to the head of the Madeline Creek basin. Exposed rock scrambling from there gains the north ridge, which leads south to the summit. The 5,700-ft north peak, the prominent point seen from the lakes, is not the top; keep it on your left. Allow about three hours from the lakes. The scrambling is class 3 for most of its length, with a class 4 chockstone move near the summit. The terrain is loose: steep duff and scree below the ridge, the chockstone gully and a boulder field, and an airy knife-edge near the top, so route-finding and care matter as much as difficulty. Car-to-car it is a very long day. A different, easier line climbs the ridge south of the peak from lower on the valley trail, but its old trail burned in 1985 and is largely gone.
Ascend the gentle glacier to the south ridge (Hogsback), negotiate a snow-filled gully through cliff bands, and scramble Class 3-4 rock via ledges on the east side of the summit ridge to the summit.
written.approach: Start at Colonial Creek Campground trailhead on SR 20 mile 130 (elevation 1,060 ft). Follow Thunder Creek Trail south for approximately 16-18 miles to Thunder Basin camp around 6,000 ft. From Thunder Basin, cross meadows and begin ascending. Traverse gradually northward around a broad ridge through open heather and high alpine terrain, gaining approximately 2 miles to reach Fremont Glacier at 8,000 feet. Campsites exist at Thunder Basin and other designated locations along the approach. The trail approach to Park Creek Pass is about 19.6 miles with 4,900 ft of gain from the trailhead; from the pass, traverse north about 2 miles across heather and alpine meadows to the Fremont Glacier at 8,000 ft.

written.beta: Ascend unstable scree slopes to reach the glacier, cross the Banded Glacier to meet the NE ridge at approximately 8,800 feet, then scramble Class 3-4 rock to the summit. The critical transition point is gaining the NE ridge on solid rock rather than attempting the summit block directly from the glacier.
Gain Douglas Glacier basin, ascend steep glacier with steeper ice/snow sections to col, traverse to meet Banded Glacier, then scramble Class 3-4 rock to summit via standard summit block.

From a Swamp Creek camp, travelers cross Swamp Creek, climb through brush and open basin to about 4,000', then work up scree and talus (with lingering snow possible) toward a roughly 7,300' notch on the southwest ridge. From the notch, a traverse below a prominent white vertical rock band on grassy ledges leads to an exposed, narrowing class 3 gully; the final ~200' to the summit climbs through loose, stacked boulders (choss).

On the ridge, follow the crest -- staying just below it to avoid small cliffs and dense subalpine trees -- to the summit. The route is entirely unmarked past Merritt Lake, so navigation, not climbing difficulty, is the main challenge. Many parties combine the peak with Mount Howard (1 mile west) as a single long day.
written.approach: From US-2 near milepost 76 (about 11.5 miles east of Stevens Pass / 24 miles west of Leavenworth), turn onto Forest Road 657 (rough, high-clearance recommended) and drive 1.5 miles to the Merritt Lake Trailhead (3,050 ft). Hike the Merritt Lake Trail up toward the ridge, connecting with the Nason Ridge Trail; figure a long day (roughly 10 miles round trip, ~4,900 ft gain for Mastiff alone) or an overnight via Merritt or Lost Lake. From Merritt Lake, follow the Nason Ridge Trail for about a mile, then turn uphill on an unsigned boot path that climbs steep forest to Mastiff's southeast ridge. Other lines reach the peak from the Crescent Lake basin via the Howard-Mastiff ridge, or up the northeast ridge from Lost Lake.

written.beta: Descend into Deception Basin, cross the stagnant, minimally-crevassed Mystery Glacier to a col (~6,700 ft) on the peak's east side, then work up mixed scree, snow, and rock on the south side of the mountain, finishing with a short, exposed Class 4 breccia section/gully to the summit block.

Mount Olson sees very few ascents. There is no recorded roped climbing route, rack, or pitch-by-pitch description for this peak anywhere; it is treated purely as a bushwhack/scramble objective by Olympic peak-baggers.

From the lakes basin, ascend the boulder field south of Little Hester Lake to gain Price's east ridge near Point 5,480'/5,440', traverse the steep north side of the ridge to a col around 5,400 ft just east of the true summit, and finish with a short ridge scramble to the 5,587 ft summit. Expect Class 3 scrambling with occasional steep snow or rock gullies on the ridge, and real routefinding difficulty — at least one party's own GPS track diverged noticeably between ascent and descent.

Rahm-to-Custer is the easier direction to routefind: follow the crest (exposed on the north side, easier scrambling on flatter rock) to a notch below Custer's final arête, then find a hidden Class 4 gully roughly 50 ft below and left of the notch to bypass the unfeasible Class 5 arête. Custer-to-Rahm is the harder direction to routefind, since the crux gully is difficult to spot from above.
First skied in 1997 by Armond DuBuque, Doug Ingersoll, Andrew McLean, and Carl Skoog.
written.approach: From Mowich Lake, hike through Spray Park and up the lower Ptarmigan Ridge to camps near 9,600 ft between the North Mowich and Edmunds glaciers, then drop to the Edmunds Glacier and the base of the headwall. The Mowich Lake road, the usual way in, has had no public access since the SR 165 bridge closed in April 2025.

written.beta: Grade II-III alpine glacier route. Climb the southern side of the glacier with multiple diagonal traverses.
Mixed alpine terrain; multiple lines/linkups exist (e.g., the East Rib, and 'Traverse of the Angels' style link-ups), but the wall as a whole is rarely climbed given the objective danger.

From Gem Lake, leave the maintained trail and traverse southwest up the ridge toward the peak. A cairn-marked traverse below cliffs near 5,400 ft leads into a small basin below the summit block, from which a class 2-3 gully of steep dirt and heather (often partly snow-filled) gains the final ~400+ ft to the 5,835 ft summit. Round trip is roughly 13 miles with about 2,700 ft of gain, commonly taking around 7 hours car-to-car; the crux is route-finding on the cairned traverse and footing in the gully when wet or snow-covered.

The standard/easiest and most commonly climbed route on Sefrit. From Ruth Creek, climbers cross the creek and bushwhack up through slide alder to the base of the 'Wall Street' couloir, a roughly 1,500-vertical-foot snow gully about 50 feet wide at 30-35 degrees. The couloir tops out on the Northwest Glacier at about 5,000 ft, crossed (roped, with pickets/flukes for crevasse hazard) to a broad saddle at 6,500 ft just west of the summit. From the saddle, parties either climb a steep, narrow chute due south to a notch just west of the summit pinnacle, or traverse southeast across a shallow snow bowl beneath the summit — the traverse exposes climbers to cornices and is usually roped with snow protection. The route finishes on the southeast ridge: a straightforward Class 2 scramble broken by about 100 ft of exposed Class 3 traversing near the middle.
Features nice mix of glacier travel and ice climbing up to 65 degrees. Connected to Crystal Glacier at upper margins.

Beyond Lake of the Angels, skirt the north/west shore and climb alpine slopes and a scree-and-snow gully (climber's-right gully) to a roughly 5,800 ft saddle at the peak's northeast/east side. From the saddle, cross scree, grass, and rock slopes southwest and scramble the southeast slope/south ridge on generally rotten, loose rock (Class 2, locally 3 to 3+) to the summit. The route has three summit horns; parties have mistaken a lower false summit for the true (south) high point. Snow lingers on the gully and saddle well into summer and is reported as firm/frail, so an ice axe is commonly carried into July.

Classed as advanced scrambling with glacier travel followed by a short Class 4 rock step. Parties rope up for the glaciated section (crevasses and a bergschrund are noted) and carry a small rock rack/runners for the final step, which is on loose, lichen-covered rock.

From Marmot Lake Camp (~4,400 ft) leave the maintained trail and follow a small creek up into an amphitheater on the west side of the peak; easy Class 1 slopes lead from the amphitheater to the summit. The multi-day approach up the Duckabush valley (roughly 21-23 trail miles one-way to Marmot Lake) is the real crux of the trip, not the summit scramble itself.

Popular with scramblers and trail runners seeking a harder version of the peak. Features Class 2-3 rock steps, steep root/dirt tread, and minor exposure, with lingering snow near the ridge crest into early summer.

From the Upper Trailhead the trail switchbacks up through old-growth hemlock/fir with a rhododendron understory, crosses a couple of seasonal streams in the first 1.5 miles, then eases into ridge walking with early views. Around 2.5 miles it reaches Camp Windy/Windy Lake amid wildflower meadows, then climbs a final steady, switchbacked pitch above treeline to the open, windswept summit plateau. There is no scrambling or hands-on terrain on the standard route; the only technical consideration is wind/weather exposure once above Camp Windy.
written.approach: Start at the Mt. Townsend Upper Trailhead (elev. ~3,300 ft), reached via Forest Road 27 off Penny Creek Road out of Quilcene — the trailhead has a small gravel lot and a Buckhorn Wilderness boundary sign where Trail #839 begins. From the lot, the trail climbs immediately into dense, heavily wooded old-growth forest via the first of three switchback sets; this opening stretch is the steepest sustained grade on the route and stays shaded most of the way. After the initial switchbacks the trail eases through forest before a second switchback section, then a third set of steep, fully sun-exposed switchbacks that break out onto the crest of a ridge — this exposed stretch is the hottest, most water-demanding part of the hike in summer, so carry all the water you need (there is no reliable creek crossing directly on-trail; the small streams crossed in the first mile or so are often dry by late summer, so shallow Windy Lake by Camp Windy is the last water).
