At about 5,300 ft, roughly 2.6 miles in, an unmarked spur trail branches off to Windy Lake/Camp Windy, a common rest stop and the last reliable flat ground before the alpine section. Continuing on the main trail, at about 5,500 ft you reach the junction with the Silver Lakes Trail #842 — stay right (straight/uphill) to continue to the summit; the left fork toward Silver Lakes involves loose, unmaintained scrambling and is not the standard route. From this junction the forest opens into subalpine meadow and the trail's grade eases considerably for the final ~1 mile to the broad, flat summit ridge (6,282 ft), passing through increasingly open wildflower meadows with the last quarter-mile crossing mostly open, low-angle grassy/rocky tundra. No technical terrain or exposure is encountered on the standard route; the main hazards are heat/sun exposure on the third switchback set, lingering snow patches on the upper meadows into early summer (which can obscure the tread and create a slip hazard on a steep sidehill), and occasional route-finding uncertainty at the Silver Lakes junction if signage is missing. Starting from the Lower Trailhead instead adds about 2 round-trip miles and roughly 500 ft of gain along the same trail corridor.

written.beta: The Northeast Ridge is the one genuinely 'moderate' way up an otherwise defended peak. From a col/bivy site above Thornton Lakes, the route crosses a shrinking glacier remnant and a loose gully to gain the ridge crest, then follows roughly 9-12 belayed pitches (mostly easy 5th class, with a runout 5.6 traverse and the signature 5.7 offwidth crux) plus short simul-climbed/scrambled sections along an exposed, towered ridge to the summit.

From a base camp or day-hike start at Watson Lakes, leave the maintained trail and work up open slopes on the mountain's north side toward the notch between the lower East Peak and the true (western) summit. Cross a short but steep snow finger / remnant glacier apron in the notch (ice axe and crampons or microspikes advisable for most of the season), then scramble loose, mossy class 3 terrain west along the south side of the ridge and along a narrow, knife-edge ridge crest to the true summit.
written.descent_text: Descent reverses the ascent line in its entirety — this is a walk-off/downclimb scramble with no rappelling (rappels: 0). From the summit, downclimb the exposed, narrow class 2-3 summit ridge (many parties use a hand line here) back down the short loose gully to the base of the summit block, then traverse back around the block and along the ridge to the 5,900-ft saddle. From the saddle, descend the east gully (the same talus/snow line used on the way up — avoid the west gully's moat/snow-bridge hazard) back into the basin above Watson Lakes, then pick up the maintained Anderson-Watson Lakes Trail #611 at the lakes for the hike out to the trailhead, passing back through the two junctions (the ~4,700-ft Anderson/Watson Lakes fork, then the Anderson Butte Trail #611.1 junction at 1 mile from the trailhead). Descent times are typically close to ascent times (roughly 3+ hours from summit to car), consistent with a straightforward if loose reversal. Descent-specific hazards: loose talus and scree in the gully below the saddle, glissade/postholing risk on residual snow into midsummer, rotten moats/snow bridges if the west-side line is mistakenly used, and route-finding across the open, unmarked basin and ridge in flat light or fog — the exposed summit-ridge downclimb remains the technical crux in both directions. Some parties instead drop east onto the shrinking Watson Glacier as a shortcut back toward the lakes.

written.beta: Above the lake the route leaves the trail, climbing through avalanche-damaged timber to treeline near 5,800 ft, then ascending loose scree and talus -- either angling toward the roughly 6,420-ft saddle between Iron Mountain and Worthington, or straight up a wide gully south of the lake -- to the peak's open summit plateau. A final short scramble up a rock fin, with some exposure, gains the true summit. Overall the route is Class 2 with a Class 3 summit block, but loose rock and off-trail routefinding make it feel harder than the grade suggests to many parties.

Mutchler Peak sits at the east end of the long southeast ridge that runs off Snowking Mountain, above the Kindy Creek/Mutchler Creek drainage. Terrain is a mix of steep heather, talus, snow/glacier remnants, and low-class rock; one documented traverse rappelled over a cornice to reach the peak.
written.approach: Park at the Cascade River Road washout roughly 14.2 miles from Marblemount, about 100 yards past the Cascade River crossing near the FR 1570 junction (signed for Kindy Ridge/Found Lake). The old FR 1570 spur is now permanently closed to vehicles, so the hike starts on the abandoned roadbed near Vee Creek at roughly 1,150-1,400 ft — parties note the washed-out culvert and downed timber (one log up to 4 ft across) blocking the road about 0.8 mile in. Follow the old road/boot path, crossing several windfalls, to an old firepit near a reliable creek (last easy water before the ridge). From the firepit the unmaintained climbers' path turns steep immediately, threading old-growth forest on exposed roots with occasional spur tracks around blowdown; expect the tread to fade into debris in places — this stretch to the Found Peak area (roughly 2.5 miles, gaining ~2,500-3,000 ft) is the main route-finding crux of the approach. The path dips to a broad saddle near 4,800 ft where the boot path is easy to lose; parties often end up scrambling 300-400 ft above the pass before relocating the trail, then follow it up through grass and boulders (~600 ft) into a meadow with Found Lake below (pools here are not reliably potable). From there the route climbs over Point 5695 and drops to a second saddle before joining Kindy Ridge proper: a broad, mostly open granite ridge combining faint tread and easy slab-hopping, steep but non-technical, with constant views toward Snowking Mountain, Mutchler Peak, and the Cyclone Lake basin. Camps are commonly made near 6,200 ft on the ridge or down at Cyclone Lake (a strikingly turquoise tarn-fed lake); a small stream south of the ridge camp and a tarn just above Cyclone Lake are the best water sources up high. From the ridge/Cyclone Lake basin, Mutchler Peak's summit block is reached by heather and blocky rock slopes rising out of the basin — moderate Class 2-3 scrambling with some loose rock near the top; no published figure gives the car-to-summit distance for Mutchler itself, but Snowking, reached by the same approach over Kindy Ridge, is roughly 16-18 miles round trip. Because the approach is entirely unmaintained (no official trail, no numbered Forest Service trail), competent off-trail navigation is required, and this is a long, full-day-plus approach — most parties treat it as an overnight rather than a single push. Other ways in: continue the Kindy Ridge approach used for Snowking's East Ridge (3rd class, Grade II) past that summit and along the connecting ridge and snowfields toward the Buckindy group, or come from the south on the longer Green Mountain, Mount Misch and Mount Buckindy traverse, camping at the pass between Kindy and Buck Creeks before crossing to Mutchler.

written.beta: The couloir has been climbed on foot (crampons) and descended on skis; above the couloir, roughly 800 vertical feet of dry, loose talus on the north ridge leads to the summit. A 2024 ascent found the snow "shockingly icy" and bypassed part of the slope by dropping right onto loose rock and scree.

First recorded climbed by Mark Bebie on September 7, 1986, who reached it by descending a couloir onto an unnamed glacier north of Primus (accessed from the North Klawatti Glacier after climbing Austera Peak the same day) and traversing to the ridge's base. The ridge took about an hour to climb once gained. It is very rarely repeated and only lightly documented.
written.approach: Same Thunder Creek Trailhead approach as the East Slope route (Colonial Creek Campground on SR 20, about 6 miles up the Thunder Creek Trail to McAllister Camp, then the climbers' trail up the ridge between McAllister and Thunder Creeks to a bivy at ~6,000 ft near the toe of the Borealis Glacier) — the North Ridge is reached by traversing around the lake instead of climbing the glacier from camp. Other parties have reached the ridge from McAllister Camp by way of Tricouni Peak's lower north ridge, or by a north-south glacier traverse between Primus and Eldorado.

written.beta: The North Ridge - West Side is one of the primary technical routes on Molar Tooth. The route ascends via the west rib with multiple short low 5th class pitches (up to 5.4), solid granite with vertical jointing, though protection is spaced in places, and enjoyable alpine climbing despite loose rock concerns.

A ridge-crest link between Cloudy Peak and North Star: from Cloudy Pass, scramble the ridge up to Cloudy Peak with expanding views toward Glacier Peak, Eldorado, and Buckner, on rock that is reasonably solid Class 4 with an option to keep it at Class 3. From Cloudy Peak, lose elevation and cross talus slopes to reach North Star, finishing on the same lichen-slicked Class 3-4 summit step as the standard route.

The West Ridge is the standard and by far the most popular route on North Twin Sister. After a long logging-road and trail approach to treeline near Dailey Prairie, the route follows the ridge crest (keeping to climber's right of the crest on the lower ridge and moving to climber's left near the false summits, to avoid the hardest moves) past two named rock features — the 'Obelisk' and the 'Cockscomb' — with a notch around 6,300 ft that bypasses a cliff band where the crest is blocked. Most of the climbing is class 3 on excellent, high-friction rock with frequent holds; a handful of class 4 (and, on the crest itself, occasional class 5) moves are encountered, and some parties rope up for a short M1b mixed step on a variation start. Multiple false summits complicate routefinding near the top.

Grade: 5.7+ YDS, Grade IV, 12 pitches, 4,000 feet. First ascent: 1963. Route: Climb partway up C-J couloir to hanging glacier on right; ascend leftmost rib to summit. Hazards: Objective danger from falling rock/ice, steep snow, exposed scrambling, avalanche potential. Best season: July-September. No bush climbing.

The Northwest Ridge is the moderate line on Colchuck Balanced Rock and the route of choice for parties who want the summit rather than the west face's hard free climbing. The line gains an obvious gully from Colchuck Lake to the notch above Jabberwocky Tower, then third-class terrain leading to the ridge proper, followed by the sharp ridge at 5.6 to the summit. Total gain from the Stuart Lake Trailhead to the summit is about 4,760 ft, and a relaxed car-to-car time is roughly 12 hours. The final obstacle is the balanced summit block itself, a short boulder problem that most parties protect. The rock is granodiorite. The peak's first ascent was made in 1958 by Gene Prater and Thomas Quin, though not necessarily by this line.

From the PCT's high point, leave it on an unsigned boot path that switchbacks up scree/talus to the northwest ridge and follows it south to the summit; the last ~50 feet is loose Class 2–3 rock with real but manageable exposure. An alternate line gains the col between Old Snowy and Ives Peak and follows the ridge crest/just-south-of-crest to the top.
Ascend the glacier, navigate crevasses and moats, then climb the exposed fourth class rock on the northeast side of the summit pyramid. Crampons and ice tools are essential.
written.approach: From the Dingford Creek Trailhead (end of FR 56, Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road), the fastest approach uses the gated continuation of the road as a mountain-bike/hike-in: roughly 7-8 miles of old roadbed (NF-5620) to Hardscrabble Horse Camp near the old Dutch Miller Gap Trailhead, saving significant time over walking it. From there, follow the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River / Dutch Miller Gap Trail (Trail 1030) east along the north bank of the river for several more miles — the tread here is in reasonable shape with minimal blowdown, passing dispersed camps and, in season, overgrown thimbleberry brush that obscures footing on the lower tread. Roughly 13-14 miles in from the trailhead (about a mile before the trail crosses toward Williams Lake/Dutch Miller Gap proper), leave the trail and ford the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River — a real ford, potentially thigh-to-waist deep and cold with snowmelt, so time it for lower water and expect wet feet. On the far side, climb steep, brushy forest into the rocky defile some parties call the 'Valley of the Chiefs,' a roughly two-mile corridor that gains the bench below Overcoat Peak. Continuous snowfields typically begin around 4,600 ft; above about 6,600 ft the route alternates between rock and snow, with one sloping, exposed rock step that requires care to downclimb onto steep snow. A common camp is on rock slabs/benches around 6,600 ft directly overlooking the Overcoat Glacier, roughly 100 ft below the glacier's toe. Total trailhead-to-camp distance is on the order of 15-16 miles with 5,000+ ft of gain; this is a serious, mostly off-trail approach through wilderness terrain (Alpine Lakes Wilderness) with real route-finding, so a GPS track or careful map work for the Valley of the Chiefs and glacier-bench section is worthwhile. From camp, traverse west across the mellow lower-angle part of the Overcoat Glacier to reach the base of a snow finger on the peak's north/east side that leads to the summit rock. Another way in follows the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River trail to Dutch Miller Gap, then bushwhacks to a basecamp at Overcoat Lake and contours over to the Overcoat Glacier.

written.beta: From the summit of Painted Mountain, follow the crest east over broken ridge and snowfields to Magenta Peak. The section from Magenta to Black Mountain is the crux: the ridge is cut by numerous gendarmes that push you off the crest to find bypasses, with at least one awkward mossy downclimb. Black Mountain, the high point of the route, has several ways up: loose scree gullies on its southeast side; a steep heather chute from the basin on its south side to a small col just west of the summit block, then a short, exposed class 3 scramble up the northwest ridge; or, harder, a class 4 corner with slabby footholds on the north side. Descend Black's south side, over lingering snow early in the season, into the basin below it toward Brown Peak, whose summit can be skipped by crossing its shoulder. Continue south to the base of Skullcap Peak and tag it, then follow easier ridge with decent use paths over the Purple Peak area to Portal Peak. Drop to Red Pass on the Pacific Crest Trail and follow the crest to White Mountain, whose south ridge has a climber's path.

Opens with a layback off a large clean flake into a long left-facing corner system with finger cracks, crosses right below a roof into a splitter crack to a mid-route ledge, then a second roof leads to a hand crack and stemming corners with a hard exit, topping out via a deep summit chimney.

A granite ridge climb with lichened overlaps, gardened dirt-filled cracks and clean tactile smears on low-angle granite; the crux comes late, on pitch 9, with an S-curved crack and bulge with smearing moves to chain anchors.

From the saddle between Vesper and Wolf Peak, an obvious ledge system cuts across the north face at roughly 5,800 ft, starting at a small notch overlooking the Vesper Glacier. The climbing is sustained low-5th-class rock with the crux exposed traverse pitch reported on pitch 5 (some parties also flag a 5.7 slab on pitch 2); belays are a mix of fixed (bolted/pin) anchors and gear anchors atop pitches 1 and 3. Popular enough that other Vesper lines (e.g. True Grit) are sometimes used as a less-crowded backup.

The final 1,000-1,100 feet ascends the west-facing slope at 30-40 degrees inclination. Most loose rock has been removed by frequent traffic. South-facing sections feature more solid red volcanic slabs. Winter ascents are possible with snow coverage on the southwest ridge when avalanche conditions are stable.
5 bolts to chains.

Parties typically approach via Twisp River Road to either the Reynolds Creek drainage (shortest, most direct) or the Williams Creek trail, then climb open basins and snowfields on the southeast side of the peak to a saddle/notch below the summit. From there, a Class 2-3 gully leads to the ridge crest, followed by a short, somewhat exposed Class 3 scramble on solid granite to the true (southeast) summit.
written.approach: From the Reynolds Creek Trailhead (~3,100–3,170 ft, reached via Forest Road 4435, which crosses the Twisp River near Mystery Campground before the Spur 4435-015 turnoff to the trailhead), the route follows Reynolds Creek Trail #402, an unmaintained, primitive Forest Service trail entering the Lake Chelan–Sawtooth Wilderness. Trail #402 climbs steadily through mixed conifer forest along Reynolds Creek for roughly 3 miles to the confluence where the South Fork of Reynolds Creek meets the main creek (approx. 4,800–5,000 ft) — parties describe scooting across a downed log to make this crossing, which can be a genuine ford in high early-season flow. This confluence is the last reliable, easy water source before the upper basin, so fill up here. Beyond the crossing, leave the maintained tread and follow the South Fork drainage, staying roughly 50 ft above the creek to avoid the worst brush and log-hopping directly in the streambed. Expect about 2 miles of intermittent bushwhacking through slide alder, downed timber, and a boot-path/game-trail tread that comes and goes — this is the route-finding crux of the approach, and parties specifically flag the numerous fallen logs and dense brush here. The drainage opens into a broad talus/scree basin around 5,500–5,700 ft directly below Reynolds Peak's southeast face and the gully/snowfield leading to its east ridge. This basin and the gully above it hold snow well into summer in most years, so carry an ice axe (and traction in early season) even on an otherwise dry-looking late-summer day. From the basin, ascend the scree, talus, and (seasonally) snow of the SE slopes/gully to a saddle/notch on the peak's east ridge, then finish with a short, exposed class 2–3 scramble (occasionally reported as harder, class 3–4, depending on snow coverage) up sound granite summit rocks to the 8,517 ft high point. An alternate, more scenic but similarly long approach exists via Williams Creek Trail and War Creek Ridge from a different Twisp River Road trailhead, but Reynolds Creek Trail #402 is the standard, shorter line. The longer Williams Creek/War Creek Ridge alternative can be combined into a loop with Abernathy Peak or Twisp Pass, running roughly 24 miles round trip with about 8,300 ft of cumulative gain. Longer alternative approaches traverse in from Williams Lake and War Creek Ridge, or from the west via Bridge Creek and Stehekin (the back way); all of them join the same southeast-side summit scramble.

written.detailed_rack: A modest rock climbing rack is essential due to poor anchor placements throughout. Bring 1-2 sets of small cams (0.4-1.5 inches) and a set of nuts for protection and rappel anchors. Many parties report difficulty finding solid rock for gear placement; natural features (trees, rocks) may be used for anchors where possible. A rope of at least 50-60 m, for rappelling the traverse.

written.beta: Climbs the middle of Roan Wall via a 5.8 bolted slab approach pitch, a 5.4 approach pitch, sustained 5.9-5.10 edge and face pitches, and a 5.11a crux slab pitch (P7), finishing with mixed 5.9-5.10- climbing. All belays feature brand-new double-ring stainless-steel bolted anchors.

bivy.name: Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac
bivy.notes: The Squire Creek road out of the west end of old Darrington has been cut by a washout well short of its historic end for many years, so the drivable road end is A moving target and the walk in to Squire Creek Wall is longer than older descriptions suggest. Parties sleeping in the car or under a tarp at the closure are doing so to get an early start on that extra walking, not because there is anything established there. Confirm the current closure point before committing — how far you can drive has changed repeatedly between seasons, and it is the single biggest variable in a Squire Creek Wall day.
bivy.water: Squire Creek runs close by and is dependable, but needs treating
bivy.permit: None for dispersed camping on forest land; the usual 14-day and setback rules apply.

bivy.name: Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County
bivy.notes: Sits in old-growth timber near where Squire Creek meets the North Fork Stillaguamish, a few miles west of Darrington on SR 530 — not on the Mountain Loop Highway, and not up the Squire Creek road itself. It is the most comfortable base for a weekend on the Darrington granite, with flush toilets and a swimmable creek, at the cost of a drive back into town each morning. Because it is county-run rather than Forest Service, the fee schedule, season and reservation window are set separately from the national forest campgrounds and should be checked on their own.
bivy.water: Piped drinking water via spigots through the campground; reliable in season
bivy.permit: None — this is a county park, not Forest Service. Nightly fee, reservations through the Snohomish County Parks system. A Northwest Forest Pass does nothing here.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 30 non-hookup sites, tents and RVs, reservable

bivy.name: Martha's Place
bivy.notes: An enormously overhung boulder near the base of the wall that offers a good camp or bivy spot.

written.beta: Features a pale slab approach pitch, face pitches with friction cruxes, corner climbing, sustained slab sections with crimpy holds, and finishes on a unique pitch combining an overlap crack with low-angle face climbing. Climbs the same very high-quality granite as the rest of Roan Wall.
written.approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north to the Arlington exit, then SR 530 east through Oso to Darrington, and turn onto Squire Creek Road at the west end of town, following it to the parking area where it's gated off by washout damage. From there the approach is long and rough: hike the old roadbed past a landslide crossing (~5 minutes in), reach the original road end around 30-40 minutes from the car, then follow a faint trail through a dry streambed and alder brush, ford Squire Creek, and pick through obscure forest track before finally breaking out into the open basin roughly 2 hours from the car. This is a known bushwhacky, unmaintained approach typical of Darrington-area crags, with route-finding (flagging, cairns) required in several spots. This route shares its approach and lower access with Center Stage. Before reaching Center Stage's start, traverse about 200 ft right to a pale slab between two obvious left-facing corners.

written.beta: From the tarn, climb the loose scree slope (snow-covered in early season) north of the tarn to a gap in the southeast ridge, then turn left (north-west) and follow the ridge about a mile over several false summits — mostly class 2 walking with a few class 3 sections and a narrow, exposed crux just below the true summit.

The finish of a longer cross-country ridge traverse rather than a stand-alone climb: from the Howard-Rock col, ascend Rock Mountain's northeast side (snow climbing and rock scrambling). Requires solid off-trail navigation and, in early season, snow-travel skills (an ice axe was necessary on a June ascent).

Climb steeply up the hillside left (east) of the boulder field to gain the northwest ridge, follow it over Point 6315', transition onto the west ridge around 5,400 ft, and finish with a scramble up the summit ridge. In snow season, cliff bands along the ridge are typically turned via snow ramps.

Approach via the maintained Hannegan Pass Trail to Hannegan Pass, then follow an unmaintained climbers' trail south onto the Ruth Glacier and up easy snow to Ruth Mountain's summit. From Ruth, descend about 1,600 ft in two roughly 800-ft steps to the low saddle between Ruth and Icy, cross talus and glacier to a notch west of Icy's Northwest Spire near 6,500 ft, then climb roughly 500 ft of 2nd-3rd class terrain and a short 4th class summit gully to Icy Peak.

Boston Basin sees less traffic and wider crevasse field on Quien Sabe Glacier compared to Sahale Glacier. Ascend left (north) side of Quien Sabe Glacier, watching for crevasses and selecting reasonable line—usually near center in steeper sections. Route between Sahale and Boston Peak summits (Sharkfin Tower is visible reference). Traverse south via col below the two peaks to reach Boston-Sahale Col. From col, traverse exposed snow to reach loose Class 3 summit scramble with persistent cornice into early summer. Final scramble is brief and loose.

written.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line: descend the northeast ridge back toward the notch/saddle below the true summit, then downclimb or rappel the short class 3/4 technical step just below the summit. Most parties rappel this step — a single 150 ft rope covers both the lead and the rappel, and the rappel itself is short, roughly 50-60 ft. This is a single rappel; no additional roped descents are reported lower on the route. Because Sheep Gap Mountain is an obscure, lightly-visited summit, no fixed bolted anchor is documented — expect to build or use a natural anchor (rock horn, chockstone, or sling around a block) rather than find bolts or chains, and bring gear/webbing to back it up or replace tat. From the base of the rappel, reverse the traverse back to Weden Pass, then retrace the talus/heather traverse and boot path down to Foggy Lake/Gothic Basin, and follow Weden Creek Trail #724 back down to Monte Cristo Road and Barlow Pass. Watch for loose rock on the class 3/4 terrain above and below the rappel and re-ford Weden Creek on the way out. Descend exactly the way you went up; a bit of temporary flagging can help you stay on line through the brushy class 3-4 terrain. Do not reuse old rappel webbing at the notch, since it is likely years old; bring your own to replace it.

written.beta: From the col between Mount Stuart and Sherpa Peak, ascend the ridge generally trending climber's left. With a 60m rope you can reach the first belay in a cave-like feature with a platform large enough for several climbers; the crux is the crack leading out of the cave (rated 5.4-5.5). A second pitch leads to another anchor, after which a short 4th-class scramble gains the notoriously airy summit block.

Climb a direct line up the consistent 45-50 degree névé and ice, deviating only briefly to skirt the bergschrund, until the angle eases near the top and a short rock/snow scramble leads to the summit.

From the Stevens Pass parking area, a route climbs past a small gray WSDOT building, under powerlines, and up a gated gravel road to Skyline Lake, then ascends northwest through timber and open slopes to a gap in the Skyline Ridge crest before following the ridge, traversing below rocky sub-points, to the summit.

From the junction, continue past a roughly 50-ft waterfall to an open meadow between Snoqualmie Mountain and Cave Ridge, then switchback up open southwest-facing slopes to the summit. Most parties treat it as a there-and-back half-day trip; it is popular as both a snow-free scramble and, with an ice axe/crampons, a winter/spring snow climb.

Traverse south past the east flank of Paul Bunyan's Stump onto the Colonial Glacier, climb ~30-degree snow to the Colonial-Neve col (~6,800-6,840 ft), then descend roughly 150-250 ft onto the Neve Glacier. Rope up and cross the Neve — parties describe the cleanest line through the center of its crevasse field — to the ridge near The Horseman on Snowfield's west side (~7,700 ft), then finish with roughly 400-600 ft of class 3-4 (occasionally class 5 on variant lines) rock scrambling to the summit.

written.detailed_rack: Pickets and slings for the glacier; minimal rock gear needed. Ice axe, crampons, and a rope with basic crevasse-rescue gear.

written.beta: Pitch 1 climbs 15 feet of 5.7 to a tree; subsequent pitches traverse ledges, include a chimney with a 5.6 downclimb, a 5.7 flake with stemming, and scrambling through boulders and trees to the top.

5.8 YDS / VI- UIAA Grade II Alpine. 5 pitches trad climbing with 4–5 technical pitches. Two 20–30 ft sections of 5.7; extensive 4th–5th class scrambling. Hazards: frequent rockfall, loose rock/choss, exposure, early-season snow/ice. Best June–August (peak July); avoid late season. First Ascent: Myhre & Sorenson (1966).

Grade 5.3-5.7, II-III Alpine. 600 vertical feet over 6 pitches from ridge base to summit. Rock quality excellent. Primary hazards: high exposure, significant glacier crevasses, late-season ice conditions, Class 4 downclimbing. 60m rope required for descent rappels. Often requires bivy camp due to multi-day approach.
written.detailed_rack: A light trad rack suffices: double-length slings for the ridge, small-to-medium nuts and cams to about 1.5 inches (tricams work well), plus full glacier travel and crevasse-rescue gear for the approach. A 60 m rope for the descent rappels.

written.beta: A 9-pitch, III, 5.8 alpine rock route established around 1985, rising in a continuous, blocky, bent line from the small glacier shared with Early Morning Spire to the summit.

From the broad saddle between Sperry and Vesper Peaks, follow the west ridge/west slope upward -- easy at first, but above a down-sloping talus and heather bench the route steepens and the exposure increases into sustained Class 3-4 terrain to the summit. Many parties combine Sperry with adjacent Vesper Peak from the same saddle in one long day.

The route climbs the ridgecrest with a brief detour onto its left side about halfway up: a ~200 ft, Class 4 first tower, then easier Class 2-3 climbing back to the ridgecrest, a 5th-class section (which is actually a downclimb off a block), then a couple more ropelengths of Class 3-4 to a false summit, and a couple more ropelengths beyond that to the true summit. Simul-climbing or moving unroped is recommended rather than pitching it out formally.

Route climbs class 2-3 scrambling to a class 4 chimney, then traverses class 3 ledges on the southeast face. Final pitch involves friction slab climbing (class 5.6) or alternate cracks left of the slab. Route-finding to the crux can be challenging. The summit horn is extremely exposed with only room for one person at a time; rope belays required for final exposed sections.

Route-finding requires staying on the correct gully (right-side route preferred over left). Traverse a ledge across the backside of the southern tower with Class 3-4 moves and occasional exposure. Navigate a slight overhang with a squeeze-through section (Class 3), then traverse the summit tower's backside to a small spur. Final approach involves either climbing a 15-foot Class 4 solid face or wrapping around the left side on Class 3 blocks to reach the summit register.

Ascend broken rock and ledges (loose throughout) toward the summit ridge; route-finding is the crux — at least one spot appears to cliff out but a cairned Class 3 crack around the corner allows passage. Continue Class 3 scrambling to the summit.

From Tailgunner Pass, scramble up Tailgunner's west ridge and south-facing scree/rock slopes to the summit dome; a narrow summit ledge is the crux and can be exposed or icy if snow lingers. In late-spring snow conditions parties have instead cramponed up a north-slope snow route and surmounted a corniced west-ridge headwall — a more technical, roped variation not represented by the Class 3 rating.
Climb the roughly 1,200-ft, up-to-35-degree couloir (crampons and ice axe, or ski crampons for splitboard/ski parties), then scramble to the NW Ridge where one 5.4 rock pitch leads to the summit.

From Thunder Basin at 5,180 feet, ascend snowfields and rocky slopes toward the summit block. The final two pitches involve Class 4 scrambling up a gully left of the summit col (approximately 85 feet to a ledge), followed by a longer pitch up a face toward a broken chimney containing a good jam crack that leads directly to the summit. Crampons and ice axe essential for snowfield sections. The route sees minimal traffic and requires solid route-finding skills.
written.descent: Reverse the route: downclimb (or rappel, if wet/loose) the broken chimney/face and gully back to the col, then descend the snow/talus back into Thunder Basin. From Thunder Basin, retrace the sheep trail down to the White River Trail junction and hike out to the trailhead. There are no fixed anchors reported on the gully/chimney — parties needing to rappel use natural anchors (horns, chockstones) and should carry extra webbing/cord. A fixed pin about 50 ft below the summit, on its north corner, is often used for the descent.

written.beta: A long, mostly non-technical mountaineering route that is more of a route-finding and stamina challenge than a climbing one. From the base-camp area near the forks of Lena Creek, climbers' paths lead up the creek drainage to a broad avalanche slope/meadow below the first cliff band; cross this and enter the couloir (snow- or rock-filled depending on season), following it up through the narrow "Hourglass" constriction near ~5,800 ft. Above the Hourglass the couloir broadens; work up and right, staying on firmer rock, then trend back left/up through loose scree to the summit. Early/mid-season the couloir holds continuous snow (ice axe and crampons required, with snow up to 40-45 degrees); by late summer it is a loose, snow-free scree-and-rock scramble.
Do not underestimate The Horn as a simple scramble: despite the modest 5.5 grade, the final summit pitch is run-out and the rock demands careful gear placement.
written.approach: Drive Hwy 101 to Hoodsport, then SR-119 (North Lake Cushman Road, becomes FR-24 past the lake) roughly 9 miles to the Staircase Ranger Station/trailhead (~800 ft) in the SE corner of Olympic National Park. Hike the North Fork Skokomish River Trail ~3.4 miles to the Spike Camp junction, then climb steeply another ~3.6 miles to Flapjack Lakes (~4,000 ft, 8 miles from the trailhead) — a limited-entry wilderness camping zone, so reserve a permit well ahead. From Flapjack Lakes, follow the Gladys Divide trail to about 4,400 ft, then leave it and climb cross-country southeast toward Sawtooth Pass to reach the base of The Fin and The Horn. Round-trip approach mileage to Gladys Divide alone runs close to 19 miles with roughly 4,000+ ft of net gain, before the additional ridge travel and the climb itself — this is realistically a backpack-in with a high camp, not a day trip from the road. From Flapjack Lakes, leave the Gladys Divide trail at about 4,400 ft, short of the divide near a small pond, and climb an open snow and rock slope southeast toward Sawtooth Pass. Snow lingers on it into midsummer, so carry an axe early in the season. Below the pass, traverse right on loose, exposed class 3-4 ground under the west face of The Fin to the notch south of The Horn.

written.beta: A crux start on below-average rock quality for Keechelus, then the route is basically over. Also toprope-able by walking up.

The East Ridge route involves vertical to overhanging rock on pitons to avoid a loose gully below, followed by approximately half a mile of alpine ridge climbing. The route was established as a first ascent during the Complete Southern Pickets Traverse in July 2003.
written.approach: From the Goodell Creek Trailhead off the North Cascades Highway (SR-20) near Newhalem, follow the Goodell Creek climbers' path, crossing two branches of the creek before a steep, cairned ascent (roughly 4 miles in) into the Terror Creek drainage. From there, either climb the steep Terror Basin route (about 2.5 miles, ~4,700 ft gain, faint tread, dense brush, and a class 3 root-pull section at a cliff band) or take the more direct but notoriously brushy Crescent Creek Basin line to reach a high camp below The Rake's east ridge. Expect a long, unmarked, bushwhack-heavy day-plus approach typical of the Pickets — there is no maintained trail. The base is reached by a snow and scree approach from the Mount Terror/Rake notch.

written.beta: Parties approach via the Snow Lakes Trail into the Core Enchantments basin, then leave the trail to ascend talus and granite buttresses on Temple's south side. The line climbs mostly class 3-4 terrain - slabs, ledges, and blocky ribs - with exposure increasing near the top, finishing with a short low-5th-class (5.3-5.6) section through a ramp/notch onto the small, airy summit. A helmet and a light rack are commonly carried for the final moves.

The talus steepens toward the Main-Middle notch, which is marked by a chockstone; from there the line traverses a broad south-facing ledge to a rock gable roughly 150 ft below the summit, then climbs a solid, enjoyable class 4 chimney directly to the top.

Seven-pitch, 800-ft Grade IV 5.12a on the east side of the tower. The route alternates bolt-protected technical slab pitches (P1, P2, P5) with crack pitches (P3, P4, P6-P7) that need a full trad rack. Rock quality is noted as inconsistent, with looser sections on P1 and the P4 roof traverse.

Eight pitches climb twin cracks, a chimney/right-facing corner, delicate face moves, and a bulging, thin-corner roof-traverse crux (P4, 5.11a) before wide cracks and chimneys and a final hand-crack/offwidth pitch reach the summit. Described by climbers as a good route that would be excellent with more traffic; some sections (notably the P6 corner) were noted as lichen-covered/dirty as of a 2018 ascent.

Vanishing Point is approximately as steep a route as one could find on the mountain—sustained, largely overhanging climbing, with most pitches at 5.11–5.12 and several at 5.10. The route was established over several years and fully modernized in 2020 with new stainless-steel anchors and improved protection. Notable features include the crux 5.12 pitch out a huge roof (pitch 11), a collapsed roof section, and several intentionally runout pitches. Published pitch counts vary between 14 and 20 depending on how the climbing is split or linked; the pitch-by-pitch breakdown here uses the 14-pitch convention.

This is the standard line up the ridge's true high point, first climbed by Fred Beckey and Herb Staley in 1952. From Burgundy Col, work north along/just below the ridge crest on 4th-class rock to a notch on the north side of the summit block, then scramble south around the west side of a large summit boulder to the base of a short low-5th-class step that gains the true summit. Most parties do it as a long day from the Washington Pass pullout, and many combine it with the neighboring Acropolis and Niki Tower to the south for an efficient multi-summit day on the ridge.

This is the primary route to Warrior Peak's Southeast Summit. From the cirque below the peak, ascend the obvious couloir between the SE and NW summits. If snow-filled (common early season), the couloir is steep and straightforward; if melted out, it's loose scree. Above the couloir, scramble to a saddle at approximately 7,000 feet, then climb steep snow or a snow moat to reach the exposed rock section. Some parties rope this short pitch; others solo it depending on conditions and skill.
written.approach: Drive Highway 101 to Sequim Bay State Park area, turn left on Louella Road for 1 mile, then left on Palo Alto Road for about 5.8 miles (it becomes FS Road 28 at the Forest Boundary), then turn right onto FS Road 2880, drive past Dungeness Forks Campground for 1 mile, stay left onto FS Road 2870 for 8.7 miles to Upper Dungeness Trailhead. Upper Dungeness Trail is the shortest and easiest approach. Hike the trail 3.4 miles and 600 feet to Camp Handy, then take the left fork and continue 3 miles and 1,850 feet to Boulder Camp (total: 6.4 miles, 2,450 feet gain). From Boulder Camp, continue south approximately 1.5-2 miles, crossing creeks, until you reach the final larger creek that flows from the cirque SE of Warrior Peak. Continue past this creek to a boulder field, then head up and back left toward the creek, staying under a band of cliffs, and continue up the boulders approximately 1 mile and 1,200 feet to reach the cirque at approximately 5,900 feet. Plan on roughly 9-10 miles of hiking to reach the base of the climb, which makes this a typical two-day backpacking objective.

written.beta: A premier alpine testpiece featuring five pitches of high-quality granite climbing to the summit terrace, plus a short sixth pitch up an easy chimney to the summit. The route climbs splitter cracks and exposed face climbing over 600 vertical feet. Pitch 2 contains the crux with thin cracks, bulbous knobs, and a small roof. The climbing features varied terrain including incipient flakes, stemming, and lieback sections. Protection is generally reliable on white granite. The onsight first free ascent in 2007 was completed with no falls.

Follow the north ridge, which dips slightly in places, to the summit pyramid. There the rock opens into many possible lines; keeping to the north (right-hand) side is easier, and there are rappel slings on the far side. Expect loose rock and choose lines carefully.
written.approach: Park on the wide paved shoulder of SR-20 about three quarters of a mile west of the signed Blue Lake trailhead lot, on the north side, where there is no guard rail. A good climbers' trail leads from the road through forest into the basin. No pass is needed at the pullout; the Blue Lake lot needs a forest pass. From the pullout, follow the climbers' trail across the basin to the notch between Whistler and Cutthroat, where the north ridge begins.

written.beta: The route climbs mostly Class 4 rock with a short Class 5 chimney partway up, on solid granite with good natural hand- and footholds, finishing with a friction-face section to the summit.
Follows the obvious long fingercrack layback corner on a buttress near Ellation. Often combined with Blood Orgy (rappel or downclimb between the two).

4-pitch trad climbing route graded 5.11a/b (also 6c/23/VIII-/E3 in other systems). Granite climbing on Cutthroat Creek Wall. Expect lichen and loose rock (first climbed in 2009 and seldom repeated). Early season may have snow/ice hazards. Rock is granite of good quality.
written.approach: From Winthrop, drive west on SR-20 for approximately 28 miles (4.5 miles east of Washington Pass). Turn right on Forest Service Road 400 and follow for 1 mile to the trailhead parking area on the left side of the road. From the parking area, hike about a quarter mile on an old roadbed and watch for cairns marking a left turn uphill. Bushwhack through the woods with no trail, gaining elevation quickly, then traverse leftward through open forest and slabby benches to the shoulder at the base of the wall's right-hand side.

written.beta: Zool Patch starts up double cracks just left of Clean Break, climbs a 5.9 offwidth flake on pitch 2, then trends left on a brushy, poorly protected traverse across blank slabs (avoided rather than climbed directly) to a pair of bail trees.
Meander up the smooth surface right of the arete, clipping one bolt, then a pin, then two more bolts.
